name: Grade 9
theme: Revelation and Scripture; Who is Jesus Christ?

lessons.title: The desire for God
lessons.idea: Human beings are religious by nature. Our longing for truth, goodness, beauty and love points beyond this world, and reason can reach God as its source. Augustine: “our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
lessons.question: What experiences in your life raise the question of God?
lessons.activity: “Wonder journal” (30 min). Students write a one-page reflection on a moment of wonder, longing or gratitude (a sunset, music, friendship). They underline the part that felt bigger than the moment. In small groups they share one sentence and look for common themes. Read Acts 17:22–28.
teach: “The desire for God is written in the human heart” (CCC 27). Humans are “capable of God” and made for communion with him (CCC 27–30). Man is a religious being.
Paul in Athens (Acts 17) begins with the Athenians’ own search: “In him we live and move and have our being.” Wisdom 13:1–9 says that from the beauty of creation we can know its author.
Reason can know God from the world and from the human person: the order of the world, conscience, the desire for happiness (CCC 31–36). It remains limited and clouded by sin (CCC 37–38).
Avoid presenting this as proof that forces belief; it is an invitation to consider.
talk: What experiences point beyond the world?
What does it mean that faith is both gift and free act?
What objection do you hear most?
quiz: Which claim does the Church make about reason and God?|Reason alone shows the Trinity|Reason is useless|Only the baptized can reason|Reason can know that God exists as the source of all, while revelation tells us who he is (CCC 36, 50)|3|CCC 36, 50–53.
The “desire for God” (CCC 27) is best described as…|Written in the human heart because we are made by and for God|Cultural only|A trick|A passing mood|0|CCC 27–30.
Paul’s speech in Acts 17 begins by…|Quoting Moses|Noting the Athenians’ search for God and quoting their poets|Condemning idols|Reading Scripture|1|Acts 17:22–28.
lessons.life: Write a one-page reflection: “What would I need to see for faith to make sense?”
lessons.saint: Augustine: the restless searcher whose Confessions begin with a prayer.
misc: “Religion is just a crutch invented by weak people.”
“If reason can reach God, we don’t need revelation.”
lessons.mem: “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” (St Augustine, Confessions 1.1)
lessons.hook: Ask students to write privately the thing they most want in life. Then ask: “Once you have it, what do you want next?” Notice the pattern of unending desire.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain in a paragraph how human desire points to God.

script.open: Write on the board: “Everyone wants to be happy.” Ask the class, “Is that true? What do people try to be happy? Does it work?” List answers: money, fame, friends, grades, games, relationships. Ask, “If all those worked, would anyone still be restless?”
teach: Say: “Human beings are the only creatures who ask ‘why?’ about everything. We look for truth, goodness, beauty and love, and we are never completely satisfied. The Catechism begins here: ‘The desire for God is written in the human heart, because man is created by God and for God.’ (CCC 27) This is not a feeling for religious people only. Almost every culture has prayer, sacrifice and some form of worship. Humans seek the transcendent.”

Say: “Augustine knew this from experience. His restless heart tried everything. Notice what it implies: if we have a hunger that nothing in this world fully satisfies, maybe we were made for more than this world. C. S. Lewis made a similar argument: ‘If I find in myself a desire which no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that I was made for another world.’ Hunger points to food, thirst to water. The desire for God points to God.”

Say: “This desire can be pushed down. We can fill our days with noise, entertainment and distraction, which Pascal called ‘diversion.’ Some people turn away from God. Others focus on pleasure, power or possessions. But the desire returns. Faith is the answer to this desire, but God first reaches out to us. In Revelation, Jesus says, ‘Behold, I stand at the door and knock.’ The call to seek God is a call to listen to our deepest longings, ask honest questions, and pray. As Jesus said, ‘Seek and you will find.’ (Matthew 7:7)”
ask: What does the Catechism say about the desire for God? (It is written in the human heart because we were made by God and for God.)
What did Augustine mean by a restless heart? (Nothing but God satisfies our deepest longing.)
What is Pascal’s idea of diversion? (We fill our lives with distractions to avoid facing the big questions.)
practice: Make a chart with three columns: What I want, How long it satisfied me, What I wanted next.
Fill in five wants.
Look for a pattern. Write a sentence about what your wants seem to be reaching for.
Rewrite Augustine’s line in your own words as a prayer.
script.close: Pray Augustine’s line quietly: “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Notice what you reach for when you are bored or lonely.”

tryit: List what you have wanted most.
Mark which wants were satisfied and for how long.
Write your own “restless heart” sentence.
lessons.saintStory:
Augustine was born in 354 in Thagaste, North Africa. His mother, Monica, was a Christian; his father, Patricius, was not. As a student in Carthage, Augustine chased fame, pleasure and wisdom. He joined a sect, took a mistress and had a son, Adeodatus. He became a professor of rhetoric, first in Carthage, then in Rome and Milan.
All the while, he felt an ache that nothing filled. In Milan, he heard Ambrose preach and began to see the faith as intellectually respectable. In 386, in a garden, he heard a child’s voice: “Take up and read.” He opened Paul’s letter to the Romans and read a line about putting on Christ. He was baptized the next Easter. He wrote Confessions about ten years later, a prayer and autobiography addressed to God.
It opens: “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” He also wrote, “Late have I loved you, O Beauty so ancient and so new.” He died in 430, as Hippo was under siege.

lessons.title: Ways to know God by reason
lessons.idea: From creation and the human person, reason can know that God exists. Thomas Aquinas’ five ways argue from motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection and order. They are arguments of reason, which faith builds on and completes.
lessons.question: What are the limits of proof for God?
lessons.activity: “Test the arguments” (35 min). In groups, read short summaries of two of Aquinas’ ways (motion and contingency). Each group states the argument in plain steps, finds one strength and one objection, and presents. Class discusses what the argument shows (a first cause) and what it doesn’t (the Trinity).
teach: The Church teaches that God can be known with certainty by natural reason (Vatican I; CCC 36). Romans 1:19–20: “his invisible nature… has been clearly perceived in the things that have been made.”

Aquinas’ five ways (Summa I, q. 2, a. 3) are about the existence of God as first mover, first cause, necessary being, source of perfection and ordering intelligence (CCC 34). They don’t describe God’s inner life.
Other paths: the cosmos, the moral law and conscience, beauty (CCC 31–34). These are “proofs” in the sense of converging reasons.
Be honest about limits: arguments do not replace faith and may fail to persuade everyone. Faith knows more than reason can reach (CCC 50).
talk: What does reasoning to God not yet tell us?
quiz: Aquinas’ “five ways” argue to God from…|Features of the world such as motion, causation, contingency, degrees and order|Scripture|Feelings|Miracles|0|CCC 34.
What do the five ways NOT prove?|That God is the first cause|That the world depends on another|That reason can reach God|The Trinity or the Incarnation, which need revelation|3|CCC 50.

Which objection do these arguments most directly face?|“An infinite chain of causes needs no first cause”|Science exists|The world has no cause|God is love|0|The reply distinguishes essentially ordered causes.
lessons.life: Summarize one argument in 100 words and test it on a friend.
lessons.saint: Anselm of Canterbury: a monk who defined theology as faith seeking understanding.
misc: “Arguments for God are all just guesses.”
lessons.mem: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims his handiwork.” (Psalm 19:1)
lessons.hook: Show a line of dominoes. “What knocked over the first one? Can the chain go back forever?” Introduce the idea of a first cause.
lessons.assess: Ask students to summarize one of the five ways and note one strength and one limit.

script.open: Write on the board three questions: Why is there something rather than nothing? Why does the universe follow laws? Why am I here? Ask students to pick the one that bothers them most and say why.
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that God can be known by reason from the created world. The First Vatican Council taught that ‘God can be known with certainty from created things by the natural light of human reason.’ (CCC 36) Paul wrote that ‘ever since the creation of the world his invisible nature… has been clearly perceived in the things that have been made.’ (Romans 1:20) Reason cannot reach everything about God, such as the Trinity, but it can show that he exists and some of what he is like.”

Say: “Thomas Aquinas gave five ways. One: motion. Things move, and each thing is moved by another, but this cannot go back forever; there must be a first mover that is not moved. Two: cause. Nothing causes itself; there must be a first cause. Three: contingency. Things exist that might not have; there must be something that exists necessarily. Four: degrees of perfection. We see that things are more or less good and true; there must be something that is perfectly good and true. Five: order. Things in nature act toward ends, like an arrow shot by an archer; there must be an intelligence that directs them. We call this God. The Catechism lists other paths: the world and the human person.”

Say: “Anselm gave a different argument. God is ‘that than which nothing greater can be thought.’ Even a person who denies God understands this idea. But something that exists in reality is greater than something that exists only in the mind. Therefore God must exist in reality. Philosophers have debated it for centuries; many find it puzzling. These arguments do not force faith, but they show that belief in God is reasonable. They clear the way. The step from ‘a first cause exists’ to ‘Jesus is Lord’ requires revelation and grace. The arguments are like a road, but faith is arriving at a person.”
ask: Can reason know God exists? (Yes, the Church teaches it can, from created things.)
Name two of Aquinas’s five ways. (Motion, cause, contingency, degrees, design.)
What does ‘faith seeking understanding’ mean? (Believing, and then wanting to understand more.)
practice: Choose one of Aquinas’s five ways, such as the argument from cause.
Write it as numbered steps: premise 1, premise 2, conclusion.
Write the strongest objection a skeptic could raise.
Write a reply, then swap with a partner and critique.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, I do not seek to understand so that I may believe, but I believe so that I may understand.” (Anselm.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Explain one argument for God to someone.”

tryit: Lay out one argument for God’s existence step by step.
Name the premise a skeptic might challenge.
Write a reply.
lessons.saintStory:
Anselm was born around 1033 in Aosta, in northern Italy. After a difficult childhood, he left home, wandered through France and joined the Benedictine abbey of Bec in Normandy. He became prior, then abbot. His students loved him. He was gentle and wise, but also a brilliant thinker.
One day he wondered whether there might be a single argument that would prove God’s existence. He had trouble eating and sleeping over the problem. Then, he said, it came to him, and he wrote the Proslogion. His motto was “faith seeking understanding” (fides quaerens intellectum): he did not try to reason in order to believe, but believed and wanted to understand more.
In 1093, he was reluctantly made archbishop of Canterbury. He clashed with two English kings, William Rufus and Henry I, over the Church’s freedom, and twice went into exile. He died in 1109 and is a Doctor of the Church.

lessons.title: Faith is reasonable and free
lessons.idea: Faith is a personal adherence to God and assent to all he has revealed. It is a gift of grace, a free act of the human person, and consistent with reason. Doubt is not the opposite of faith but can lead to deeper faith.
lessons.question: Does faith require certainty? Do doubts mean unbelief?
lessons.activity: “Doubt conversation” (35 min). A structured conversation. Read John 20:24–29 and Mark 9:24. Questions: What did Thomas need? What did Jesus give? What is the difference between doubt and unbelief? What helps when I doubt? Students write one honest question for God, and one step to seek an answer.
teach: Faith is “a personal adherence of man to God… and a free assent to the whole truth that God has revealed” (CCC 150). It is a supernatural gift that precedes our decision (CCC 153–155).
Faith is reasonable: there are signs of credibility (miracles, prophecies, the Church’s holiness) (CCC 156). Faith and science do not conflict (CCC 159).
It is also free: no one can be forced to believe (CCC 160, 2106). Doubt can be voluntary (a refusal) or involuntary (a difficulty); the second is not a sin (CCC 2088).
Hebrews 11 lists the faithful. Faith grows through prayer, sacraments and community (CCC 162).
talk: What is the difference between doubt and unbelief?
What do you do with unanswered questions?
quiz: Faith in the Catechism is…|Blind trust|A feeling|A personal adherence to God and assent to all he has revealed, a gift of grace and a free act (CCC 150, 153–155)|Opinion|2|CCC 150, 153–155.

The father in Mark 9:24 prays “I believe; help my unbelief.” What does this show?|Faith can coexist with difficulty and still ask for grace|Faith excludes doubt|Doubt is sin|He had no faith|0|Mark 9:24; CCC 2088.
Voluntary doubt differs from involuntary doubt in that the former…|Is a deliberate refusal to hold what is revealed (CCC 2088)|Is rare|Is harmless|Is a difficulty|0|CCC 2088.
lessons.life: List three questions you have about faith and take one to a trusted catechist or priest.
lessons.saint: Thérèse of Lisieux: a young nun who kept believing in the dark.
misc: “Having doubts means I’ve lost my faith.”
lessons.mem: “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is trusting a friend reasonable? Is it free?” Both. Faith in God is like trust, but supernaturally given.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define faith and distinguish doubt from unbelief.

script.open: Ask, “Is faith the same as a guess? Is it believing something with no evidence? Or is it more like trusting a friend?” Take answers. Let several disagree.
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that faith is both reasonable and free. Faith is a gift of God, a grace, and it is also a human act. The Catechism says ‘Believing is possible only by grace and the interior helps of the Holy Spirit. But it is no less true that believing is an authentically human act.’ (CCC 154) Faith is not contrary to reason. John Paul II began his encyclical Fides et Ratio, ‘Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth.’ A bird needs two wings.”

Say: “What are the reasons for faith? God’s revelation is accompanied by ‘proofs’: miracles, prophecies fulfilled, the holiness and growth of the Church, her stability, and above all the Resurrection of Jesus. These are called motives of credibility. They do not make faith a conclusion of logic, but show that it is reasonable to trust. Then, because the truths of faith go beyond what we see, we trust God’s word. We believe, not because we understand, but because God, who cannot deceive, has spoken. Faith is a trust, like trusting a doctor or a friend.”

Say: “Faith is also free. God never forces. Jesus said, ‘If any man would come after me…’ The Church teaches the right to religious freedom: no one should be forced to believe, because faith must be a free response. Faith also grows. It can be tested, as Thérèse’s was. Doubt is not the same as unbelief; the father in Mark 9:24 said, ‘I believe; help my unbelief!’ Honest questions are welcome; Thomas questioned and was answered. Persistent, willful denial is different. How do we grow in faith? Pray, read Scripture, receive the sacraments, ask questions, find good friends and serve others.”
ask: Is faith opposed to reason? (No; they are two wings.)
What are motives of credibility? (Signs and reasons that make faith reasonable.)
Is doubt a sin? (Honest doubt is not; willful rejection is different.)
practice: Draw a table: Reasons for faith / Trust in God / My free choice.
Under each, list items: the Resurrection and witnesses, the Church’s history and saints, my experience of prayer, a decision to keep going.
Mark what you can check and what you must decide.
Write one honest question you have and who you could ask.
script.close: Pray: “I believe; help my unbelief.” (Mark 9:24.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask a trusted adult a question you have about faith.”

tryit: Sort reasons for faith into evidence, trust and choice.
Mark what you can check and what you must decide.
Write what makes faith free.
lessons.saintStory:
Thérèse spent nearly all her short life in faith without any struggle. She had been a joyful child and wrote about God with simple confidence. But in April 1896, the year before she died, she began to have a severe trial of faith. Suddenly the thought of heaven, which had been so sweet, was blocked by a thick fog. She wrote that she heard a voice mocking her: heaven does not exist, there is nothing after death.
She did not stop praying. She wrote that she made constant acts of faith, even when she felt nothing. She said she was sitting at the table of sinners and unbelievers, eating their bread of sorrow, offering it for them. In her last weeks, suffering from tuberculosis, she kept going, saying, “I have never given the good God anything but love.”
She died on September 30, 1897. Her doubts were not a lack of faith but a place where faith was tested. She is a Doctor of the Church.

lessons.title: Revelation in history
lessons.idea: God reveals himself in history, in deeds and words that explain each other, step by step. He speaks through creation, to Adam and Noah, Abraham, Moses and the prophets, and finally in his Son Jesus Christ, who is the fullness of revelation.
lessons.question: Why a gradual revelation?
lessons.activity: “Build a timeline” (30 min). Students build a timeline of revelation: creation, Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, prophets, Jesus, apostles. For each, add the event, God’s self-disclosure (e.g., his name at the burning bush) and the Scripture reference. Read Hebrews 1:1–2.
teach: Revelation is God’s self-communication (CCC 50–53). He does it by deeds and words intimately connected (CCC 53, 2). It unfolds in stages (CCC 54–64).
Christ is the fullness: “No one has ever seen God; the only Son… has made him known” (John 1:18; CCC 65–66). There will be no new public revelation after the apostles (CCC 66).
“Private revelations” (e.g., Fatima, Lourdes) do not add to the deposit of faith; they help us live it (CCC 67).
The response to revelation is the obedience of faith (CCC 142–143).
talk: What is public vs private revelation?
quiz: The “fullness” of revelation is…|The Bible alone|The Church fathers|Moses|Jesus Christ (Hebrews 1:1–2; CCC 65)|3|CCC 65–66.
God reveals himself through…|Deeds and words intimately connected (CCC 53)|Philosophers|Dreams|Words only|0|CCC 53.
Private revelations such as Fatima or Lourdes…|Add to the deposit of faith|Are required belief|Contradict Scripture|Do not add to revelation but may help us live it (CCC 67)|3|CCC 67.
lessons.life: Read Hebrews 1:1–4 and write a summary.
lessons.saint: John of the Cross: a Carmelite who wrote poems from a prison cell about God’s approach to the soul.
misc: “God revealed himself only through the Bible.”
lessons.mem: “In many and various ways God spoke of old to our fathers by the prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son.” (Hebrews 1:1–2)
lessons.hook: Show a photo album arranged chronologically. “What do you learn about a person by seeing how they act over time?” God teaches us himself through history.
lessons.assess: Ask students to place five stages of revelation in order and explain how Christ is the fullness.

script.open: Draw a long arrow from left to right on the board. Say, “God’s revelation unfolds like a story. Mark where you think the key moments are, from Adam to Jesus.” Let students place sticky notes or marks, then compare with the lesson.
teach: Say: “Revelation means God revealing himself and his plan. We cannot climb up to God; he has to come to us. The Catechism says: ‘God, who “dwells in unapproachable light”, wants to communicate his own divine life to the men he freely created.’ (CCC 52) He does it in stages, ‘by deeds and words,’ in history. This is called the economy of revelation, or salvation history. The Bible is the record, but the revelation is mainly God’s action and word in history.”

Say: “The stages. One: in creation, God reveals himself through the world. Two: to Adam and Eve, God gave a promise after the fall, the first Gospel (Genesis 3:15). Three: to Noah, a covenant with all creation. Four: to Abraham, who was called to be the father of a people. Five: to Moses and Israel, at the Exodus and Sinai, God revealed his name and gave the Law. Six: through the prophets, who called Israel back and gave hope of a new covenant. Seven: in Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh. ‘In many and various ways God spoke of old to our fathers by the prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son.’ (Hebrews 1:1-2)”

Say: “Christ is the fullness of revelation. There will be no new public revelation after him and the apostles. The Church speaks of the end of public revelation with the death of the last apostle. This doesn’t mean that nothing new is learned: the Church grows in understanding. Private revelations, such as apparitions at Lourdes or Fatima, do not add to the faith, but help people live it. The Church may approve them as worthy of belief but never requires belief. God also reveals himself in a personal way in prayer. As John of the Cross said, Christ is the whole of God’s word.”
ask: What is revelation? (God revealing himself and his plan.)
Who is the fullness of revelation? (Jesus Christ.)
Do private revelations add to the faith? (No; they help people live the faith.)
practice: Draw a timeline from creation to Christ with seven stops.
Under each, write the person or event, and what God revealed about himself.
Circle where it reaches its fullness.
Write a sentence: “God revealed himself gradually because…”
script.close: Pray the opening of Hebrews 1: “In many and various ways God spoke of old.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read Hebrews 1:1-4 aloud.”

tryit: Trace the stages of revelation on a timeline.
Name who God spoke through at each.
Mark the fullness.
lessons.saintStory:
John was born in 1542 in Fontiveros, Spain, to a poor family; his father died when he was young. He worked in a hospital, and then entered the Carmelites. He met Teresa of Avila, who asked him to help her reform the order, and he became a leader of the “discalced,” or barefoot, Carmelites.
Opponents in the unreformed order kidnapped him in December 1577 and locked him in a tiny cell in Toledo for nine months. It was dark, hot in summer and freezing in winter. He was beaten and given little food. In that cell, he composed some of the great poems in the Spanish language, including part of the Spiritual Canticle. He escaped through a window in August 1578.
He wrote The Ascent of Mount Carmel and The Dark Night of the Soul. He taught that God reveals himself fully in Christ: “In giving us his Son, his only Word, God spoke everything to us at once in this sole Word, and he has no more to say.” He died in 1591 at forty-nine.

lessons.title: Sacred Tradition and Scripture
lessons.idea: Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition flow from the same divine source and together form one sacred deposit of the Word of God. Tradition is the living transmission of the Gospel in the Church, not a list of old customs.
lessons.question: How are Scripture and Tradition related?
lessons.activity: “Two streams” (30 min). Students analyze 2 Thessalonians 2:15, 2 Timothy 2:2 and John 21:25 to find the role of spoken and written teaching. Write a one-page summary: What is Tradition? What is Scripture? How do they relate?
teach: “Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture are bound closely together… they flow out of the same divine wellspring” (CCC 80–82; Dei Verbum 9). Together they form the deposit of faith (CCC 84).
The apostles handed on what they received orally and in writing (CCC 75–79). Not everything Jesus said and did was written (John 21:25), and the Church’s living Tradition preserves the whole.
Tradition includes doctrine, liturgy, the Creed, Church Fathers and the Magisterium (CCC 78). It must be distinguished from ecclesiastical traditions, which can change (CCC 83).
Show the difference from sola scriptura: the canon itself was decided by the Church’s Tradition.
talk: What would be lost without Tradition?
What would be lost without Scripture?
quiz: “Sacred Tradition” in Catholic teaching is…|A second Bible|Local habit|Old customs|The living handing on of the Gospel by the apostles and their successors (CCC 78)|3|CCC 75–79.
Which would NOT be part of the deposit of faith?|A diocesan fasting rule (a changeable discipline)|The Creed|The Real Presence|The Trinity|0|CCC 83.
2 Thessalonians 2:15 matters in this lesson because it…|Forbids writing|Rejects tradition|Defines infallibility|Commends both spoken and written apostolic teaching|3|2 Thessalonians 2:15.
lessons.life: Find three Christian practices not explicit in Scripture (e.g., the canon, Sunday).
lessons.saint: Vincent of Lérins: a monk who asked how we know what is truly Catholic.
misc: “Tradition is man-made customs that contradict the Bible.”
lessons.mem: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by letter.” (2 Thessalonians 2:15)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How do you know what your great-grandparents were like?” Written letters and stories told within a family. Both are needed.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how Scripture and Tradition relate and give an example.

script.open: Hold up a Bible and a catechism. Say, “Which came first, the book or the community?” Take a vote and listen to reasons. Say, “The answer shapes how Catholics read the Bible.”
teach: Say: “God’s revelation is handed on in two ways, called Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture. Vatican II’s Dei Verbum says they ‘flow from the same divine wellspring’ and ‘merge into a unity and tend toward the same end.’ (DV 9) Sacred Scripture is the word of God written down under the Holy Spirit. Sacred Tradition transmits the word of God, entrusted to the apostles by Christ and the Holy Spirit, to their successors, so that they may preserve, expound and spread it. The Church accepts both with equal devotion and reverence.”

Say: “Some Christians say ‘Scripture alone’ (sola scriptura). Catholics respond: where does the Bible say that? Paul wrote, ‘Stand firm and hold to the traditions which you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by letter.’ (2 Thessalonians 2:15) John wrote that Jesus did many other things not written (John 21:25). The Church existed before the New Testament was written, and it was the Church that determined which books belong in the Bible. Tradition tells us what books are Scripture, and how to read them. Examples of Tradition not explicit in Scripture: the canon of the Bible, Sunday worship, infant Baptism, the Trinity’s terminology.”

Say: “Tradition (capital T) is not the same as traditions (small t). Capital T Tradition is the apostolic teaching, which cannot change. Small t traditions are customs, devotions and disciplines that vary by time and place, like the Rosary, the Latin Mass, or fasting practices; they can change. Vincent’s test helps to tell the difference: universality (everywhere), antiquity (always), consensus (by all). Today, the Church’s teaching authority, the Magisterium, interprets both. The three work together. Without Tradition, the Bible is read without context; without Scripture, Tradition would drift.”
ask: How is revelation handed on? (Through Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition.)
What is the difference between Tradition and traditions? (Apostolic teaching vs. changeable customs.)
What is Vincent’s test? (What has been believed everywhere, always, by all.)
practice: Make a list of items: the Trinity, Sunday Mass, the Rosary, infant Baptism, meatless Fridays in Lent, the sign of peace, the Assumption.
Sort into Tradition (apostolic teaching) and traditions (customs).
For each Tradition, find a source in Scripture and in the early Church (use the Catechism’s index).
Write one sentence explaining your sorting.
script.close: Pray the Creed. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask someone where their faith traditions came from.”

tryit: Apply Vincent’s test to three doctrines.
Find where they appear in Scripture and the Fathers.
Say what is Tradition and what is only custom.
lessons.saintStory:
Vincent was a monk on the island of Lérins, off the coast of southern France, in the fifth century. The monastery was a center of study and prayer; Honoratus founded it, and many bishops trained there. Vincent had been a soldier and a man of the world before becoming a monk.
In about 434 he wrote a short book, the Commonitory, under the name Peregrinus (“pilgrim”), for those who wanted help in recognizing the true faith amid many teachers. His rule: hold “what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all.” He also wrote that the faith can grow, as a body grows from child to adult, without changing its nature: “Let there be progress, but let it be real progress, not change of faith.”
We know little else about him. He died before 450. His simple test is still quoted in Church documents.

lessons.title: The Magisterium
lessons.idea: The Magisterium is the Church’s teaching office, the Pope and the bishops in union with him, who authentically interpret the Word of God. It is a servant of the Word, not above it. Teaching comes with different levels of authority and calls for different levels of assent.
lessons.question: What does infallibility mean (and not mean)?
lessons.activity: “Levels of assent chart” (35 min). Students build a chart: (1) dogmas defined as divinely revealed, requiring the assent of faith; (2) definitive doctrines requiring firm acceptance; (3) authoritative non-definitive teaching requiring religious submission of mind and will; (4) prudential decisions. Give examples at each. Read Matthew 16:18–19 and John 21:15–17.
teach: The Magisterium interprets the Word of God authentically (CCC 85–87). Its authority is exercised by the Pope and bishops (CCC 888–892).

Infallibility: when the Pope speaks ex cathedra, or the bishops in an ecumenical council define a doctrine of faith or morals, they are preserved from error (CCC 891). The Pope is not infallible in everything.
The faithful give “the obedience of faith” (CCC 143). The sense of the faithful also has a role (CCC 91–93).
Dissent and development: doctrine can develop in understanding but not contradict (CCC 94).
talk: How do you respond to non-infallible teaching?
quiz: The Magisterium’s relation to the Word of God is that it…|Replaces it|Competes with it|Serves it, teaching only what has been handed on (CCC 86)|Stands above it|2|CCC 86.
Which teaching calls for “the assent of faith”?|Opinions|Local policies|Prudential advice|A dogma defined as divinely revealed (CCC 88–89)|3|CCC 88–89, 891.
Infallibility applies to…|Definitive teaching on faith and morals by the Pope or the bishops with him (CCC 891)|Any statement|Weather|Politics|0|CCC 891.
lessons.life: Read the Catechism’s sections on Magisterium (85–95).
lessons.saint: Robert Bellarmine: a Jesuit cardinal who explained the Church’s authority with patience and clarity.
lessons.mem: “He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me.” (Luke 10:16)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who decides what a rule in a game means when players disagree?” A referee. The Church has one for the faith, serving the rule, not making it.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe infallibility and give an example at each level of assent.

script.open: Ask, “Who decides the rules of a game when there is a disagreement? Why must there be a referee? What would happen without one?” Take answers. “Jesus knew the Church would need an authority.”
teach: Say: “The Magisterium is the Church’s living teaching office: the Pope and the bishops in communion with him. Jesus gave this authority to the apostles: ‘He who hears you hears me.’ (Luke 10:16) ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.’ (Matthew 18:18) He promised that ‘the Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth.’ (John 16:13) The Magisterium is not above the word of God, but serves it, ‘teaching only what has been handed on.’ (DV 10)”

Say: “Catholics speak of infallibility. This means that, by the Holy Spirit’s assistance, the Church cannot err in teaching a matter of faith or morals when it is definitively proposed. It is exercised in three ways. One: the Pope speaks ex cathedra (‘from the chair’), as shepherd of all Christians, defining a doctrine on faith or morals to be held by the whole Church. This has been done rarely: for example, the Immaculate Conception (1854) and the Assumption (1950). Two: the college of bishops, in union with the Pope, in an ecumenical council, such as Nicaea or Vatican II. Three: the ordinary and universal Magisterium, when the bishops all over the world, in union with the Pope, agree on a teaching as definitive. Infallibility doesn’t mean the Pope is sinless or right about everything. He can be wrong about science, politics or personal opinions.”

Say: “There are different levels of teaching. Dogmas must be believed by divine and Catholic faith. Definitive teachings must be firmly held. Authoritative non-definitive teaching, such as encyclicals and the Catechism, requires ‘religious submission of mind and will.’ (LG 25) Prudential judgments, such as how to handle a political problem, are not binding in the same way. Catholics are invited to study, ask questions and discuss. But the Church asks us to give a docile and trusting response. The Magisterium gives us stability. In a world of constant opinions, we know we are not left alone.”
ask: Who forms the Magisterium? (The Pope and the bishops in union with him.)
Does infallibility mean the Pope is sinless? (No; it concerns defined teaching on faith and morals.)
Give an example of an infallible definition. (The Immaculate Conception; the Assumption.)
practice: Prepare cards: Resurrection of Christ, the Assumption, an encyclical on the environment, the Pope’s opinion on a football team, the Nicene Creed, a bishop’s letter on a local issue, the Catechism.
Sort by level of authority: dogma, definitive, authoritative teaching, opinion or prudential.
Discuss one that surprised you.
Write what each level asks of a Catholic.
script.close: Pray for the Pope and bishops. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look up when the Assumption was defined.”

tryit: Sort teachings into infallible and non-infallible.
Say who can teach each.
Write what it asks of us.
lessons.saintStory:
Robert Bellarmine was born in 1542 in Montepulciano, Italy, to a family related to Pope Marcellus II. He joined the Jesuits at eighteen, against his father’s wishes. He was small and bright, a gifted preacher, and became a professor at Louvain and Rome. He wrote Disputations on the Controversies of the Christian Faith, a clear, fair-minded defense of Catholic teaching against Protestant arguments, so careful that even Protestants cited it. He also wrote a catechism used for centuries.
He was made a cardinal in 1599, and served as a Vatican adviser. In 1616, he was the one who delivered to Galileo the Church’s warning about teaching the Sun-centered system as established fact. Bellarmine said that if there were a real proof, the Church would need to reinterpret the Scriptures. But there was no proof yet.
He lived simply as a cardinal and gave his money to the poor, and died in 1621. He is a Doctor of the Church.

units.title: Scripture: the word of God
units.eq: How do we read the Bible well?

lessons.title: Inspiration and truth
lessons.idea: God is the author of Scripture and the human authors are true authors. Inspiration means the Holy Spirit moved them to write what he wished. The Bible teaches without error the truth God wanted for the sake of our salvation.
lessons.question: What does “without error” cover?
lessons.activity: “Two creation accounts” (30 min). Compare Genesis 1:1–2:4 and 2:4–25. Students list differences in order and style and the common teaching (God is Creator; humanity is made in his image; creation is good; marriage). Ask what each form of truth the author intends.
teach: Inspiration: the Holy Spirit is the author of Scripture, with human authors acting as true authors (CCC 105–107). 2 Timothy 3:16: “All Scripture is inspired by God.”
Inerrancy: the books teach “firmly, faithfully and without error that truth which God, for the sake of our salvation, wished to see confided to the Sacred Scriptures” (CCC 107; Dei Verbum 11).
This does not mean the Bible is a science textbook, nor that every statement in any sense is to be taken literally. We must ask what the author intended (CCC 109–110).
The Church also teaches that all of Scripture is a unity because of one divine author (CCC 112).
talk: What is the purpose of Scripture?
quiz: Inerrancy means…|The Bible is a dictation|Every sentence is a science fact|The Scriptures teach without error the truth God wished to put there for our salvation (CCC 107)|There is no human author|2|CCC 107.
God and human authors of Scripture relate as…|God is author and humans are true authors who used their own faculties (CCC 106)|God dictated and humans copied|Angels|Humans only|0|CCC 105–106.
To understand a biblical text we must ask…|Only the dates|What we feel|Nothing|What the author intended, considering literary form and time (CCC 109–110)|3|CCC 109–110.
lessons.life: Read Genesis 1 and Psalm 104 side by side.
lessons.saint: Gregory the Great: a pope who called Scripture a letter from God to his creature.
misc: “Inerrancy means the Bible answers every scientific question.”
lessons.mem: “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness.” (2 Timothy 3:16)
lessons.hook: Present two maps of the same city: a street map and a subway map. “Both are true; they serve different purposes.” Scripture teaches the truth God wanted for salvation.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain inspiration and inerrancy with the creation accounts as example.

script.open: Read aloud a passage from the Bible, but don’t say what it is. Then say, “Who wrote this? Several answers are correct.” Let students answer. “Today we make sense of that.”
teach: Read 2 Timothy 3:16-17 and 2 Peter 1:20-21. Say: “All Scripture is ‘breathed out by God.’ The Church teaches that God is the author of Scripture. The Holy Spirit inspired human authors, who wrote as true authors, using their own faculties and abilities. Dei Verbum 11 says: ‘Everything asserted by the inspired authors or sacred writers must be held to be asserted by the Holy Spirit.’ So the Church holds that the books of Scripture ‘firmly, faithfully, and without error teach that truth which God, for the sake of our salvation, wished to see confided to the Sacred Scriptures.’”

Say: “Notice the phrases. ‘Without error’ is called inerrancy. It applies to what the sacred authors intend to teach for our salvation, not to every detail of history or science. The Bible is not a science textbook, nor does it always give precise measures; it can use round numbers, symbolic language, and imprecise memory. If the Bible tells a parable, the truth is the lesson, not the facts of the story. What the author affirms is true. But we must know what the author affirms, which is why we study the literary forms and context.”

Say: “Some people misunderstand inspiration in two directions. One thinks God dictated every word, like a secretary taking dictation, so human authors contribute nothing; this is fundamentalism. The other thinks the Bible is only human religious literature, with no divine authorship. The Catholic position is both: God is the principal author; the human authors are real authors. It parallels the Incarnation: Christ is fully divine and fully human; Scripture is God’s word in human words. Gregory’s idea of a letter helps: a letter from God, written through a person, addressed to each of us.”
ask: Who is the principal author of Scripture? (God, the Holy Spirit.)
What does inerrancy cover? (What the sacred authors affirm for the sake of our salvation.)
What is fundamentalism? (Reading every word as dictated and literal, ignoring human authorship and literary form.)
practice: Read Dei Verbum 11 together.
Underline what it says about God and about human authors.
Draw a diagram with God, the Holy Spirit, a human author, and the text, showing how they relate.
Write a one-paragraph answer to: “Is the Bible without error?”
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you have written me a letter. Help me to read it.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the Bible as a letter for a week.”

tryit: Read 2 Timothy 3:16 and Dei Verbum 11.
Write what is taught without error.
Explain how God and the human author both write.
lessons.saintStory:
Gregory was born around 540 into a wealthy Roman senatorial family. He became prefect of Rome, then gave up his career, turned his house into a monastery and gave his fortune to the poor. He wanted a quiet monastic life, but the Church needed him. He was sent as an ambassador to Constantinople, and in 590 was elected pope, at a time when plague, floods and invasions threatened Rome.
He called himself “servant of the servants of God,” a title popes still use. He organized food for the poor, defended Rome, and sent Augustine and forty monks to England in 596. He wrote many sermons and letters on Scripture. In one, to a physician, he asked, “What is Scripture but a kind of letter from almighty God to his creature? If an earthly king sent you a letter, you would not rest until you had read it. The Emperor of heaven has sent you a letter for your life, and yet you neglect to read it.”
He died in 604. He is a Doctor of the Church, and Gregorian chant is named for him.

lessons.title: Interpreting Scripture
lessons.idea: The Church gives three criteria for interpreting Scripture: attend to the content and unity of the whole Bible, read it within the living Tradition of the Church, and keep in mind the analogy of faith. Alongside the literal sense there are three spiritual senses.
lessons.question: What are the three criteria?
lessons.activity: “Practice on Exodus 14” (35 min). Students apply the criteria to the crossing of the Red Sea: literary form and context (history, liturgical retelling), unity (Isaiah 43, 1 Corinthians 10:1–2), Tradition (Easter Vigil, Baptism), analogy of faith (God saves). Then identify the spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, anagogical).
teach: CCC 112–114 sets three criteria: content and unity, living Tradition, analogy of faith. Complementary: literary genre, the author’s intention, historical context (CCC 109–110).
The literal sense is the foundation (CCC 116). The spiritual senses are: allegorical (how events signify Christ), moral (how to act), anagogical (our heavenly destiny) (CCC 115–117).
A medieval couplet summarizes: “The letter teaches what happened, allegory what you should believe, the moral what you should do, anagogy where you are heading.”
Exegetes are to work “so that, as it were by previous study, the judgment of the Church may mature” (CCC 119).
quiz: Which is one of the three criteria for interpreting Scripture (CCC 112–114)?|Individual intuition|Attend to the unity of the whole Scripture|The majority|The newest scholarship only|3|CCC 112.
The “anagogical” sense of Scripture points to…|Allegory|Our eternal destiny|Moral conduct|The literal event|1|CCC 117.
The literal sense is…|Allegory|Unimportant|The meaning the words convey, on which the spiritual senses build (CCC 116)|The only sense|2|CCC 116.
lessons.life: Practice the four senses on one verse.
lessons.saint: Bonaventure: a Franciscan teacher who showed how Scripture speaks on many levels.
misc: “A spiritual reading means ignoring the plain meaning.”
“The Church forbids reading the Bible critically.”
lessons.mem: “Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.” (Luke 24:45)
lessons.hook: Show a passage out of context (a movie quote edited). Ask: “What happens when we remove context?” Scripture needs context too.
lessons.assess: Ask students to apply the three criteria to a short passage.

script.open: Show a picture of an onion or layered cake and ask, “What does it mean to say the Bible has layers?” Then read Exodus 14 (the Red Sea) briefly, and ask, “What is this passage about? Is there more than one answer?”
teach: Say: “Dei Verbum gives three rules for reading Scripture as it was written: be attentive to the literary forms; be attentive to the unity of the whole of Scripture; and read it within the living Tradition of the Church, guided by the analogy of faith. The first level of interpretation is the literal sense: the meaning intended by the human author, discovered by careful study of language, context, genre and history. All other senses are based on the literal. It would be wrong to build a spiritual meaning on a misunderstanding of what the text says.”

Say: “The Church also speaks of the spiritual senses, which are meanings intended by God, the author, beyond the literal. There are three. The allegorical sense: we can see the significance of events by seeing how they point to Christ. The crossing of the Red Sea is a sign of Christ’s victory and of Baptism. The moral sense: events are written for our instruction, to lead us to act justly. ‘These things happened to them as a warning, but they were written down for our instruction.’ (1 Corinthians 10:11) The anagogical sense (from the Greek for ‘leading up’): events point to our eternal destiny. Jerusalem in the Bible is a sign of the heavenly city.”

Say: “Let’s see them with the word ‘Jerusalem.’ Literally, it is a city in Palestine. Allegorically, it is the Church. Morally, it is the soul that is at peace with God. Anagogically, it is the heavenly Jerusalem. Notice that the New Testament itself reads the Old Testament this way. Paul in Galatians 4 reads Hagar and Sarah as allegory. Jesus says that Jonah is a sign of his burial. Not every passage has all four, and these senses can’t be used arbitrarily; they must agree with the faith of the Church. We also should be careful to avoid reading our own preferences into the text. The Church’s liturgy and the Fathers are good guides.”
ask: What are the two main kinds of sense in Scripture? (Literal and spiritual.)
Name the three spiritual senses. (Allegorical, moral, anagogical.)
What is the foundation of all senses? (The literal sense.)
practice: Choose a short passage, such as the Exodus crossing (Exodus 14:21-31) or Jonah in the fish.
Write four sentences: what happened (literal), how it points to Christ or the Church (allegorical), how it teaches me to live (moral), and where it leads (anagogical).
Check the Catechism or a Catholic Bible footnote for support.
Share with a partner.
script.close: Pray the Collect from the Sunday Mass or: “Open our eyes to the wonders of your law.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Try the four senses on a Sunday reading.”

tryit: Interpret one passage in four senses.
Write each sense in a sentence.
Compare with the literal.
lessons.saintStory:
Bonaventure was born in 1221 in Bagnoregio, Italy. According to a family story, as a child he was gravely ill, and his mother prayed to Francis of Assisi, and he recovered. Bonaventure later joined the Franciscans and studied in Paris, where he taught alongside Thomas Aquinas. He was a brilliant theologian, but humble. Once, when two visitors from the pope came to deliver his cardinal’s hat, they found him washing dishes. He asked them to hang the hat on a tree until he was finished.
In 1257, he was elected minister general of the Franciscans, and he guided the order through a troubled period, writing the official life of Francis. He believed that studying should lead to prayer. His book, The Soul’s Journey into God, takes the soul step by step from creation to contemplation.
He commented on Scripture, finding in it a many-layered meaning. He was made a cardinal in 1273 and died in 1274 during the Council of Lyon. He is a Doctor of the Church, the “Seraphic Doctor.”

lessons.title: The canon and its formation
lessons.idea: The canon is the list of inspired books. The Church, guided by the Spirit, recognized 46 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books by the late fourth century (Hippo 393, Carthage 397; confirmed by Popes). Protestants removed seven Old Testament books (the deuterocanon).
lessons.question: Who decided and why?
lessons.activity: “Canon research” (35 min). Students use a timeline of canon formation (Muratorian Fragment c. 170, Athanasius’ Easter letter 367, Hippo 393, Carthage 397, Innocent I 405, Florence 1442, Trent 1546). In pairs, they prepare an answer to a Protestant objection: “The Apocrypha was not in the Hebrew canon.” Use evidence: the Septuagint, New Testament quotations, Christian use.
teach: The Church discerned the canon through her Tradition and the Spirit’s guidance (CCC 120). The 73 books include seven deuterocanonical books (Tobit, Judith, 1–2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch) and additions to Esther and Daniel.
The earliest Christians used the Greek Septuagint, which included these books. Luther moved them to an appendix in 1534. The Jewish canon was fixed later (c. 90–100 AD), after Christianity separated.
Peter notes Paul’s letters as “Scripture” (2 Peter 3:15–16). The New Testament canon was stable by the fourth century based on apostolic origin, orthodoxy and universal use.
The Church honors Jewish tradition. Discuss respectfully.
quiz: The deuterocanonical books are…|Added at Trent without precedent|Seven Old Testament books in the Greek Septuagint that Catholics keep (CCC 120)|Apocrypha rejected by Catholics|New Testament letters|1|Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees.
Which council in 393 listed the canon?|Ephesus|Hippo|Nicaea|Trent|1|Hippo 393, Carthage 397.

A reply to “the Catholic Church added books” is that…|They were part of the Greek Bible used by early Christians, and Luther moved them in 1534|It did|They are unimportant|They were invented|0|Septuagint usage.
lessons.life: Read a short passage from Wisdom or Sirach.
lessons.saint: Damasus I: the pope who asked Jerome for a Bible and helped fix the list of books.
misc: “The Catholic Church added books to the Bible.”
lessons.mem: “Our beloved brother Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom given him… in all his letters.” (2 Peter 3:15–16)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who decided which books belong in the Bible?” Take guesses. “It was not decided in a single stroke or by one person.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to give three facts that support the Catholic canon.

script.open: Spread out the table of contents of a Catholic Bible and a Protestant Bible. Ask students to find the differences in two minutes. Collect their findings on the board.
teach: Say: “The canon is the official list of books that make up the Bible. The word means ‘rule’ or ‘measure.’ The Catholic canon has 73 books: 46 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. The Church did not invent the canon, but discerned which books were inspired by the Holy Spirit. She used criteria: apostolic origin or connection; use in the liturgy and teaching of the churches; agreement with the rule of faith; and wide acceptance. By the late second century, most of the New Testament was in common use. Four Gospels were established early: Irenaeus said there could be neither more nor fewer than four.”

Say: “The first list with exactly our 27 New Testament books is from Athanasius in 367. Local councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397, 419) approved the list, with the Pope’s approval. The Council of Trent in 1546 formally defined the canon, in response to Reformers who had rejected some books. The seven Old Testament books that Protestants omit (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1 and 2 Maccabees, plus parts of Esther and Daniel) are called deuterocanonical, ‘second canon.’ They were in the Greek Septuagint, the Bible used by Jesus’ contemporaries and the early Church. Martin Luther removed them from the Old Testament because they were not in the later Hebrew Bible, which was fixed by the Jewish rabbis around AD 90-100, after Christianity had begun.”

Say: “There were also writings that the Church rejected, often called apocrypha, such as the Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Judas and the Gospel of Peter. These were written in the second century or later, often under apostles’ names, and contain ideas that conflict with apostolic teaching (for example, gnostic ideas about matter being evil). The Church’s test was whether they were handed on from the apostles. The Da Vinci Code story, that the Council of Nicaea decided the Bible, is false; Nicaea did not discuss the canon. The canon shows that the Bible does not stand alone: the Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, recognized the inspired books. Scripture and the Church’s authority are linked.”
ask: How many books are in the Catholic Bible? (73.)
Who defined the canon formally? (The Council of Trent in 1546, after earlier councils and lists.)
What are deuterocanonical books? (Old Testament books in the Greek Septuagint not in the Hebrew Bible.)
practice: Give students a chart of the books of the Bible in a Catholic and in a Protestant canon.
Highlight the differences.
Write the criteria the Church used.
Write a three-sentence answer for a friend who asks: “How do you know the Bible books are the right ones?”
script.close: Pray: “Lord, thank you for the gift of the Bible.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look up the deuterocanonical books in your Bible.”

tryit: Read the canon lists and compare.
Mark the seven disputed books.
Explain who decides which books are Scripture.
lessons.saintStory:
Damasus was born around 305, perhaps in Spain or Rome, and became pope in 366. His election was disputed by a rival, and rioting in Rome led to many deaths. Once secure, he worked to strengthen the Church’s unity and its identity. He restored the catacombs and the tombs of martyrs, and composed inscriptions in verse for them.
In 382, he held a council in Rome, which many scholars connect to a list of the books of Scripture. He also invited Jerome, the greatest biblical scholar of the day, to Rome as his secretary, and asked him to produce a standard Latin Bible by revising the Old Latin translations. This became the Vulgate.
Damasus helped establish the place of the Roman see as the leading church, using the phrase “apostolic see.” He died in 384. His support for Jerome’s work shaped how the Church read the Bible for a thousand years.

units.title: The Old Testament and Christ
units.eq: How is Christ in the Old Testament?

lessons.title: Unity of the two Testaments
lessons.idea: The two Testaments form one story. The Old prepares for Christ and is fulfilled in him; the New is hidden in the Old. Typology — persons and events that foreshadow Christ — is the key to reading them together.
lessons.question: How is the New hidden in the Old?
lessons.activity: “Typology table” (30 min). Fill a table: type (Adam, Noah’s ark, Isaac, Passover lamb, manna, bronze serpent, Jonah, Temple), New Testament reference and fulfillment. Add one sentence on what the type teaches about Christ. Read Luke 24:44–47.
teach: “The Old Testament is a preparation for the New” (CCC 128). “The New Testament is hidden in the Old and the Old is unveiled in the New” (St Augustine; CCC 129).
Typology is the Church’s ancient method: Adam is a type of Christ (Romans 5:14), Noah’s flood of Baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21), the manna of the Eucharist (John 6:32).
The Old Testament keeps its own value (CCC 121–123). Marcion’s rejection was condemned. The Church honors the Jewish people’s covenant, which God has not revoked (CCC 839–840; Romans 11:29).
Warn against supersessionism: the Church does not teach that Jews have been replaced.
talk: How are the two Testaments one?
quiz: “The New is hidden in the Old and the Old is unveiled in the New” is from…|Pius X|Augustine|Luther|Aquinas|1|CCC 129.
A type is…|A mistake|A symbol of nothing|A prophecy only|An Old Testament person, event or thing that foreshadows Christ|3|CCC 128–130.
Which pairing is a type and fulfillment?|Moses and Nero|Adam and Christ (Romans 5:14)|David and Pilate|Noah and Herod|1|Romans 5:14.
lessons.life: Make a type–antitype chart with five rows.
lessons.saint: Melito of Sardis: a bishop who traveled to the Holy Land to learn the books of the Old Testament.
misc: “The Old Testament God is angry and the New Testament God is loving.”
lessons.mem: “Everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled.” (Luke 24:44)
lessons.hook: Show the first half of a mystery novel, then the last page. “The ending makes the beginning make sense.” Jesus is the ending that makes sense of the whole story.
lessons.assess: Ask students to give three types and their fulfillments.

script.open: Show an architect’s model or blueprint and a picture of a finished building. Ask, “Is the blueprint false once the building is made? Is the building possible without it?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Some early heretics, like Marcion in the second century, said the Old Testament God was an angry, lesser god, and that Christians should throw it away. The Church rejected this. The Old Testament is the word of God and is part of the Bible. The same God of the Old Testament is the Father of Jesus. The Catechism says: ‘The Old Testament is an indispensable part of Sacred Scripture. Its books are divinely inspired and retain a permanent value.’ (CCC 121) Jesus himself prayed the psalms and read the prophets. We call them one story in two parts.”

Say: “Augustine’s phrase is helpful: ‘The New Testament is hidden in the Old; the Old is made manifest in the New.’ The Old Testament prepares for Christ. It reveals God’s plan, shows human need for salvation, and teaches about God, prayer and justice. The New Testament fulfills it. It does not abolish it. Jesus said, ‘I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.’ Examples: Adam and Christ (Romans 5), the Passover lamb and the Lamb of God, manna and the Eucharist, the Temple and Jesus’ body, the old covenant and the new covenant.”

Say: “Some say the Old Testament is violent. It does include difficult passages: wars, harsh laws. The Church teaches that revelation is gradual and that God was educating a people. Some passages reflect the ancient world’s values and are not an endorsement of violence. We read them in the light of Christ, who is the fullness. And the Jewish people remain beloved by God: Paul wrote, ‘The gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.’ (Romans 11:29) The Church condemns antisemitism, and recognizes the Jewish people as our ‘elder brothers’ (John Paul II). The covenant with Israel has not been revoked.”
ask: Why does the Church keep the Old Testament? (It is God’s inspired word and prepares for Christ.)
What did Marcion teach? (That the Old Testament should be rejected; the Church condemned it.)
How does the New fulfill the Old? (It completes and reveals the meaning of what was promised.)
practice: Make a matching chart: Old Testament item / New Testament fulfillment.
Include: Adam / Christ; Passover lamb / Lamb of God; manna / Eucharist; Jonah / Resurrection; Temple / Christ’s body; Melchizedek / Christ the priest.
Add the verses.
Write a sentence explaining why we need both Testaments.
script.close: Pray Psalm 119:105: “Your word is a lamp to my feet.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read an Old Testament passage and look for Jesus.”

tryit: Match Old Testament and New Testament pairs.
Explain how the New fulfills the Old.
Say why the Church keeps both.
lessons.saintStory:
Melito was bishop of Sardis, in what is now Turkey, in the second century. He was widely respected and wrote many works, but most are lost. In one, he mentions that he traveled to the East, to the place where the Scriptures were preached and where the events happened, in order to learn accurately the books of the Old Testament. He gave a list of them, the earliest Christian list we have, which includes all the books of the Hebrew Bible except Esther.
His surviving work is a Paschal Homily, On Pascha, a great Easter sermon. In it he pictures the Old Testament as a sketch, a model that the artist makes before the final statue. When the real thing is complete, the model is no longer needed, but it had its role. “The model was precious before the reality, and the parable was wonderful before its interpretation. But when the church arose and the Savior appeared, the model was emptied, having yielded its power to the reality.”
He died in about 180.

lessons.title: Covenant history
lessons.idea: God forms a people through successive covenants: with Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David and finally the new covenant in Christ. Each covenant expands the family of God, and Jeremiah promised a new one written on hearts.
lessons.question: What is new in the new covenant?
lessons.activity: “Covenant chart” (35 min). Plot the covenants with: partner (family, tribe, nation, kingdom, all), sign (Sabbath, rainbow, circumcision, Law/Sabbath, throne, Eucharist), promise and Scripture. Read Jeremiah 31:31–34 and Luke 22:20 and note the fulfillment.
teach: Covenant with Adam (creation, Hosea 6:7), Noah (Genesis 9), Abraham (Genesis 12; 15; 17), Moses (Exodus 19–24), David (2 Samuel 7), the new covenant (Jeremiah 31; Luke 22:20) (CCC 56–64).
Each covenant widens the circle: a married pair, a household, a tribe, a nation, a kingdom, all peoples (Scott Hahn’s “family” model). Each includes oath, sign and blessings and curses.
The new covenant is “everlasting” (CCC 66). The Eucharist is its sacramental sign (CCC 1365).
Link to the unity of salvation history.
talk: What is new in the new covenant?
quiz: The new covenant is promised in…|Jeremiah 31:31–34|Psalm 1|Genesis 1|Daniel 7|0|Fulfilled in Luke 22:20.
Which covenant sign matches Noah?|Circumcision|Tablets|Throne|Rainbow|3|Genesis 9:12–17.
Covenants in Scripture differ from contracts because they…|Create family bonds with oaths|Are private|Have no signs|Are only legal|0|CCC 56–64.
lessons.life: Read Hebrews 8–9.
lessons.saint: Ruth: a foreign widow whose loyalty made her the great-grandmother of David.
lessons.mem: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” (Jeremiah 31:33)
lessons.hook: Say: “A covenant is a family bond. Each time God widens it.” Draw circles that grow: family, tribe, nation, world.
lessons.assess: Ask students to chart three covenants with partner, sign and promise.

script.open: Write on the board the word ‘contract’ and ask for examples. Then write ‘covenant’ and ask students to describe the difference. Use their ideas to introduce the Bible’s covenants.
teach: Say: “A covenant is a sacred bond that establishes a family relationship, with promises and signs, sealed with an oath or a ritual. It is more than a contract. A contract exchanges goods and services; a covenant exchanges persons: ‘I will be your God, and you shall be my people.’ The Bible is the story of God’s covenants, each a step in the plan. They show God’s fidelity: he keeps his word even when we break ours.”

Say: “The covenants: With Adam, the covenant of creation, in which God made man in his image (Genesis 1-2). With Noah, God promised never again to destroy the earth by flood; the sign is the rainbow. With Abraham, God promised land, descendants and blessing to all nations; the sign is circumcision. With Moses at Sinai, God gave the Law, and Israel became a priestly kingdom and holy nation; the sign is the Sabbath. With David, God promised that a son of David would reign forever (2 Samuel 7), the promise of the Messiah. And the new covenant, promised by Jeremiah, which is fulfilled by Christ.”

Say: “In each covenant, God makes the first move, and the people often fail. The prophets denounce Israel’s unfaithfulness as adultery. Yet God does not abandon. Hosea shows a husband who keeps loving a faithless wife. In Jeremiah 31, God promises a new covenant, with a law written on hearts, and forgiveness of sins. At the Last Supper, Jesus said, ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood.’ The Eucharist makes us members of the covenant. Baptism is the sign. The new covenant doesn’t cancel the older covenants but completes them. And God’s covenant with the Jewish people is still valid.”
ask: What is a covenant? (A sacred bond that makes a family relationship.)
What was the sign of the covenant with Noah? (The rainbow.)
What is the new covenant? (Established in Christ’s blood, with a law written on hearts.)
practice: Draw a table with six rows: Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, Christ.
Fill in columns: the promise, the sign, what the people failed to do, what God did.
Under the last row, write how Christ completes the others.
Write a short summary: “God’s covenant love shows that…”
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you are faithful; make us faithful.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the book of Ruth; it’s four short chapters.”

tryit: Trace the covenants on a chart.
Mark each one’s sign and promise.
Write how Christ completes them.
lessons.saintStory:
Ruth was a Moabite woman, from a people who were Israel’s enemies. She married an Israelite man who had come to Moab with his family during a famine. Her husband died, as did her husband’s brother and father, leaving three widows: Naomi, Ruth and Orpah. Naomi decided to return to Bethlehem, and urged her daughters-in-law to go home. Orpah went back. Ruth said, “Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you; for where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”
In Bethlehem, Ruth gleaned grain in the fields, and met Boaz, a relative of Naomi’s husband, who treated her with great kindness. He acted as her kinsman-redeemer and married her. Their son Obed was the father of Jesse, the father of David. So Ruth, a foreigner, became an ancestor of David and of Christ. She appears in Matthew’s genealogy.
Her story shows hesed, covenant loyalty, which is a theme of God’s dealing with Israel.

lessons.title: Prophecy and fulfillment
lessons.idea: The prophets announced the Messiah: born of a virgin in Bethlehem, a king from David’s line, a suffering servant, entering Jerusalem humbly. Jesus fulfills these promises, and the Gospels show it.
lessons.question: How was Jesus the fulfillment?
lessons.activity: “Study five prophecies” (35 min). Pairs examine Isaiah 7:14 / Matthew 1:22–23, Micah 5:2 / Matthew 2:5–6, Isaiah 53 / 1 Peter 2:24, Psalm 22 / Matthew 27, Zechariah 9:9 / Matthew 21:4–5. For each: context in the original, what the New Testament sees, and a caution (not every connection is literal).
teach: Messianic prophecy is part of the preparation for Christ (CCC 522–524, 702–716). Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) mean “anointed one.”
The Gospels use many Old Testament texts to show Jesus’ identity. Some are direct predictions (Micah 5:2), others typological or deeper meanings (Hosea 11:1 / Matthew 2:15).
Isaiah 53 is read by the Church as the Servant who suffers for sins (CCC 601). Psalm 22 begins with the cry Jesus uttered on the Cross.
Be fair to Jewish readings of these passages and to critical questions about translation (e.g., almah in Isaiah 7:14 translated parthenos in the Septuagint).
talk: How do you respond to “vague” objections?
quiz: Micah 5:2 foretells…|The birthplace of the Messiah, Bethlehem|The Ascension|The flight into Egypt|The Passion|0|Matthew 2:5–6.

A caution about messianic proofs is that…|There are none|Some fulfillments are typological or deeper meanings rather than literal predictions|They are unimportant|All are literal|1|e.g., Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15.
Isaiah 53 is read by the Church as…|The Servant who suffers for sins (CCC 601)|A war song|A description of Cyrus|A genealogy|0|CCC 601.
lessons.life: Choose five prophecies and trace the New Testament fulfilments.
lessons.saint: Anna the prophetess: an old widow who recognized the child in the Temple.
lessons.mem: “But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel.” (Micah 5:2)
lessons.hook: Say: “Imagine if someone predicted details of your life 700 years before you were born.” Introduce Micah 5:2.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present two prophecies with their fulfillments and one caution.

script.open: Ask, “If someone made a prediction years ago that came true in detail, how would you react? What if there were dozens?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Old Testament is full of promises that look forward. The Catechism says that Christians read the Old Testament ‘in the light of Christ crucified and risen.’ (CCC 129) Prophecy is not just predicting the future; the prophets also called Israel to faithfulness. But they also gave promises of a Messiah, and the New Testament shows Jesus as their fulfillment. Jesus himself said so: ‘Everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled.’ (Luke 24:44)”

Say: “Some prophecies. Born of a virgin: Isaiah 7:14 / Matthew 1:23. Born in Bethlehem: Micah 5:2 / Matthew 2:1-6. Called out of Egypt: Hosea 11:1 / Matthew 2:15. A herald in the wilderness: Isaiah 40:3 / Mark 1:2-4. A king on a donkey: Zechariah 9:9 / Matthew 21:5. Betrayed for thirty pieces of silver: Zechariah 11:12-13 / Matthew 26:15. Pierced hands and feet, garments divided: Psalm 22 / John 19. A suffering servant who bears our sins: Isaiah 53 / 1 Peter 2:24. Not one bone broken: Psalm 34:20 / John 19:36. A Son of Man who comes with the clouds: Daniel 7 / Mark 14:62.”

Say: “How do we evaluate this? Some objections: Jesus’ followers may have shaped the story to fit. But some things, like birthplace or crucifixion, can’t be arranged. Some prophecies had a first meaning in their own time and a deeper meaning later (a ‘fuller sense’). The point is the pattern: the whole Old Testament leads toward Christ in many ways, like pieces of a puzzle that fit. The convergence is the strongest evidence, not one single verse. And we should be careful not to treat the Old Testament as only prediction: it has its own meaning. Together they give a coherent story that God has been preparing. The fulfillment invites faith, but doesn’t force it.”
ask: What did Jesus say about the Old Testament? (It was written about him and must be fulfilled.)
Name one prophecy and fulfillment. (Bethlehem; virgin birth; suffering servant.)
Why does the pattern matter? (Many pieces converge on Christ.)
practice: Build a chart of ten prophecies with their Old Testament and New Testament verses.
Beside each, rate it: very specific, somewhat specific, or general.
Choose the two you find strongest and explain why.
Write a short reply to a friend who says the Gospel writers made it up.
script.close: Pray the Nunc Dimittis: “Lord, now let your servant depart in peace.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Learn Simeon’s prayer; the Church says it every night.”

tryit: Chart ten prophecies and fulfillments.
Rate each by how specific it is.
Explain why the pattern matters.
lessons.saintStory:
Anna was a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was eighty-four years old, and had been married only seven years before she was widowed. Since then, she lived in the Temple in Jerusalem, “worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day.”
When Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the Temple to present him to the Lord, as the Law required, the old man Simeon took the baby in his arms and blessed God: “My eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples.” At that very hour, Anna came up, gave thanks to God, and spoke about the child to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem.
Simeon and Anna are the last figures of Old Testament waiting. After long hope, they saw the promise come true. Luke places her at the opening of the Gospel to show that prayer and fasting prepared Israel for the Messiah.
