units.eq: Who do you say that I am?

lessons.title: The historical Jesus
lessons.idea: The Gospels are reliable historical witnesses to the Jesus who lived. Beyond the Gospels, ancient writers such as Tacitus, Josephus and Pliny mention him. The evangelists wrote within decades of the events, using eyewitness testimony.
lessons.question: What do non-Christian sources say?
lessons.activity: “External testimony” (30 min). Students read short excerpts from Tacitus (Annals 15.44), Josephus (Antiquities 18.3 and 20.9), Pliny the Younger (Letter 10.96), and compare them to Gospel details. Make a list of what independent writers confirm (crucified under Pilate, followers called Christians, worshiped as God).
teach: The Church holds that the Gospels “faithfully hand on what Jesus … did and taught for the eternal salvation of men” (CCC 126; Dei Verbum 19). They are history shaped by faith.

Manuscript evidence: thousands of early copies, the earliest fragments within decades (P52, c. 125 AD). The Gospels were written within about 30–70 years of the events, while eyewitnesses lived (Luke 1:1–4).
Non-Christian sources: Tacitus, Josephus (parts debated), Pliny, Suetonius. Few scholars today doubt that Jesus existed and was crucified under Pilate.
Faith is not just history; but faith is not against history.
talk: What is the criterion of embarrassment?
quiz: Which source outside Christianity mentions Jesus’ execution under Pilate?|Plato|Virgil|Tacitus (Annals 15.44)|Homer|2|Tacitus c. 116.
The earliest New Testament manuscript fragments date from…|The second century (e.g., P52)|The Middle Ages|The Reformation|The tenth century|0|P52 c. 125.
Luke 1:1–4 shows the Gospel’s method as…|Dream|Rumor|Myth|Careful investigation of eyewitness testimony|3|Luke 1:1–4.
lessons.life: Read Tacitus and Josephus excerpts.
lessons.saint: Matthew: a tax collector who left his table to follow Jesus.
misc: “There’s no evidence outside the Bible that Jesus existed.”
lessons.mem: “It seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you.” (Luke 1:3)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How do historians know about Julius Caesar?” By documents, manuscripts and other sources. Apply the same tools to Jesus.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present three pieces of evidence for the historical Jesus.

script.open: Pose a challenge: prove that a person from 2,000 years ago existed. What evidence would count? List it on the board. Say, “Now let’s apply the same standard to Jesus.”
teach: Say: “The vast majority of historians, including non-Christians, agree that Jesus of Nazareth was a real person. Outside the Bible, we have mentions. Tacitus, a Roman historian, around AD 116, wrote that ‘Christus’ was executed by Pontius Pilate under Tiberius, and that his followers in Rome were persecuted by Nero. Josephus, a Jewish historian, around AD 93, mentioned Jesus and James, his brother, and John the Baptist (some of the longer passage was probably edited by Christians, but a core is original). Pliny the Younger wrote to Emperor Trajan around AD 112 about Christians who sang hymns to Christ ‘as to a god.’ Suetonius and the Jewish Talmud also mention him. Not a single ancient source denies he existed.”

Say: “The Gospels are our main source. They were written within 40 to 70 years of the events, which is early for ancient history, by people who knew eyewitnesses. Paul’s letters, written in the 50s, describe Jesus’ death, Resurrection and the Last Supper, and he met Peter and James. We have thousands of manuscripts: over 5,800 Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, some from the second century, which is far more than any other ancient work. The Gospels include embarrassing details that the writers would not invent: Peter denying Jesus, the disciples fleeing, a crucified Messiah, women as first witnesses.”

Say: “What do historians generally accept? Jesus was baptized by John. He preached the kingdom of God, taught in parables, and performed healings and exorcisms that people attributed to him. He gathered disciples, including twelve. He was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Soon after, his followers claimed he was risen from the dead, and many suffered for it. Historians disagree about the meaning, but the Church’s faith is rooted in history. As the Catechism says, we believe in a real person who lived at a particular time and place. Luke wrote, ‘It seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account.’”
ask: Name one non-Christian source for Jesus. (Tacitus, Josephus, Pliny.)
How many Greek New Testament manuscripts survive? (Over 5,800.)
What embarrassing details support the Gospels’ reliability? (Peter’s denial, the disciples fleeing, women as first witnesses.)
practice: Make a chart: Source, Date, What it says about Jesus.
Include Tacitus, Josephus, Pliny, Paul and the Gospels.
Add a column: Independent of Christian sources?
Write a three-sentence summary of what we can know about Jesus from history.
script.close: Pray: “Lord Jesus, you are real and present. Help me to follow you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read Tacitus’s mention of Christ online with a parent.”

tryit: Collect sources outside the Bible that mention Jesus.
Mark what each says.
State what historians agree on.
lessons.saintStory:
Matthew, also called Levi, was a tax collector in Capernaum, collecting taxes for the Romans and Herod Antipas. Tax collectors were hated as traitors and cheats. One day, Jesus walked by Matthew’s booth and said, “Follow me.” Matthew got up and followed him. That evening, he threw a banquet at his house for Jesus and many other tax collectors and sinners. The Pharisees complained. Jesus replied, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Matthew was one of the Twelve. Early Christians wrote that he composed a Gospel, first for Jewish Christians, and that he preached in Judea before going to other lands. We don’t know for certain how he died.
His background as a tax collector, used to keeping records, may explain why his Gospel is so organized. He gathers Jesus’ teaching into five great discourses, like the five books of Moses.

lessons.title: True God and true man
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, one divine Person with two natures, human and divine, without confusion or division. Councils from Nicaea to Chalcedon defended this against heresies.
lessons.question: Why does it matter that Jesus is both?
lessons.activity: “Councils and heresies” (35 min). Match each heresy to the council and the truth defended: Arianism (Nicaea 325), Apollinarianism (Constantinople 381), Nestorianism (Ephesus 431), Monophysitism (Chalcedon 451), Monothelitism (Constantinople III 681). Write a one-sentence summary of Chalcedon’s formula.
teach: Chalcedon (451): “one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, only-begotten, in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation” (CCC 467).
Jesus has a human body, soul, intellect and will (CCC 470–483). He is not a human person with a divine mask but the divine Person who assumed human nature.
The Philippians hymn (2:5–11) describes the self-emptying of the Son. “Emptying” is not losing divinity but taking the form of a servant.
Take care to connect doctrine to devotion: because God became man, our humanity is redeemed (CCC 460).
quiz: Chalcedon taught that Christ is…|One nature|Two persons|One divine Person in two natures, divine and human|A creature|2|CCC 467.
Docetism taught that Christ…|Was truly human|Only seemed to have a body|Was a man|Was divine|1|CCC 465.
Why does it matter that Christ is truly human?|He needed to learn|It is poetic|Because only a true man could save mankind from within (CCC 470–478)|It does not|2|CCC 470–478.
lessons.life: Read the Chalcedonian definition.
lessons.saint: Cyril of Alexandria: a bishop who defended Mary as Theotokos, Mother of God.
misc: “Jesus only became God after the resurrection.”
lessons.mem: “Though he was in the form of God, [he] did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself.” (Philippians 2:6–7)
lessons.hook: Read Philippians 2:5–11. Ask: “What does it mean that he ‘emptied himself’ and still remained God?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Chalcedon’s formula and one heresy it rejected.

script.open: Draw two overlapping circles on the board. Label one ‘God’ and the other ‘human.’ Say, “If Jesus is both, where do the circles meet?” Let students suggest what goes in the overlap.
teach: Say: “The Church believes that Jesus is true God and true man. The first Christians believed it from the start (John 1:1, 14; Philippians 2:6-8; Colossians 2:9), but it took centuries to say it clearly, as errors arose. The heresies are mirror errors. Docetism: Jesus only seemed to be human. Arianism: Jesus is not fully God but a created being; condemned at Nicaea in 325. Apollinarianism: Jesus had no human mind. Nestorianism: Jesus is two persons, a divine and a human, joined together; condemned at Ephesus in 431. Monophysitism: Jesus’ human nature was absorbed into the divine, so he has only one nature; condemned at Chalcedon in 451.”

Say: “Chalcedon taught: Jesus is ‘truly God and truly man, consisting of a rational soul and a body; consubstantial with the Father in his divinity, and consubstantial with us in his humanity; like us in all things except sin.’ He is one Person in two natures, ‘without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.’ Later, the Third Council of Constantinople in 681 added that he has two wills, divine and human, which are in harmony. Jesus’ human will freely follows his divine will, as in Gethsemane.”

Say: “Why does this matter? If Jesus is not fully God, he can’t save us or reveal God. If he is not fully man, he can’t represent us or truly die for us. Gregory of Nazianzus said, ‘What is not assumed is not healed.’ Because Jesus is one Person, we can say that God was born, God suffered and God died. This is why Mary is Theotokos: the child she bore is God. It’s about Jesus, not just Mary. We should not think of Jesus as God pretending to be man, or as a man with divine help. He is both, entirely. We pray to him as a divine Person, and he knows our life from within.”
ask: What does Chalcedon say about Jesus? (One Person in two natures, divine and human.)
Why is Mary called Theotokos? (The child she bore is God.)
What did Nestorius teach? (That Jesus is two persons.)
practice: Prepare a chart: Heresy, What it taught, What it denied, Church’s response.
Include Docetism, Arianism, Apollinarianism, Nestorianism, Monophysitism.
Rewrite the Chalcedon formula in plain English.
Write a short explanation for a friend: “Why does it matter that Jesus is fully God and fully man?”
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary, pausing at “Mother of God.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Explain to someone why Mary is Mother of God.”

tryit: Match each heresy to its error and the Church’s answer.
Mark what Chalcedon said.
Explain the doctrine in your own words.
lessons.saintStory:
Cyril became patriarch of Alexandria in 412. He was a strong, sometimes fierce leader, and an outstanding theologian. In 428, Nestorius, the patriarch of Constantinople, objected to calling Mary Theotokos, “God-bearer” or Mother of God, saying she should be called Christotokos, “Christ-bearer,” because she was the mother of Christ’s human nature only. Cyril saw that this split Christ into two persons.
He wrote to Nestorius, and appealed to Pope Celestine, who backed him. In 431, the Council of Ephesus met. Cyril presided for the Pope. The council affirmed that Jesus is one Person, the Son of God, and that Mary is the Mother of God, not because she is the source of his divinity but because the child she bore is God.
When the news reached Ephesus, the people reportedly filled the streets with torchlight celebrations. Cyril died in 444. He is a Doctor of the Church.

lessons.title: Jesus’ self-understanding
lessons.idea: Jesus’ words and deeds show who he understood himself to be: he forgave sins, claimed to be Lord of the Sabbath, called God his Father, and said “I AM.” Either he was what he claimed or something else; the Church believes he is the Son of God.
lessons.question: What did Jesus claim?
lessons.activity: “I AM sayings” (30 min). Collect Jesus’ seven “I AM” sayings in John (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way/truth/life, vine) and “Before Abraham was, I am” (8:58). Students note which Old Testament images each echoes and which title (Messiah, Son of God, Son of Man, Lord) fits.
teach: Titles: Christ (Messiah), Son of God, Son of Man, Lord (CCC 436–455). “Son of Man” (Daniel 7:13–14) is Jesus’ own preferred title, expressing both humanity and divine glory.
Jesus claims divine prerogatives: forgiving sins (Mark 2:5–7), authority over the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), calling God “Abba” (Mark 14:36).
C. S. Lewis’ “trilemma” (liar, lunatic, Lord) is a popular argument but should be used carefully, since it omits “legend.” Consider the evidence on the Gospels’ reliability.
Faith in Christ’s divinity is a gift as well as a conclusion.
talk: What does it mean to follow?
quiz: In Mark 2, forgiving sins was a claim of divine authority because…|Only God can forgive sins (Mark 2:7)|It was routine|It was symbolic|Priests do it|0|Mark 2:5–10.
“Son of Man” in Jesus’ usage evokes…|A rabbi|Daniel 7’s figure given dominion by God, a title of glory|A mere human|A simple phrase|1|Daniel 7:13–14.
Which “I AM” saying echoes the divine name?|“Blessed are the poor”|“Follow me”|“Come and see”|“Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58)|3|John 8:58.
lessons.life: List Jesus’s “I AM” sayings in John.
lessons.saint: Thomas the apostle: the doubter who made the greatest confession of faith.
lessons.mem: “I and the Father are one.” (John 10:30)
lessons.hook: Read Mark 2:1–12. Ask: “What is the objection of the scribes? Is it reasonable?” Only God can forgive sins.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list three ways Jesus claimed divine authority and explain their significance.

script.open: Ask, “If someone said, ‘I am God,’ what would you think? What would you want to see?” Take answers. “Jesus made claims that people couldn’t ignore.”
teach: Say: “Jesus did not call himself ‘God’ in so many words in the Gospels, but his claims point to it. He spoke with authority: ‘You have heard that it was said… but I say to you.’ He forgave sins: when he told the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ the scribes said, ‘Who can forgive sins but God alone?’ (Mark 2:7) He said, ‘Before Abraham was, I am.’ (John 8:58) The listeners picked up stones, since they understood he was using God’s name. He said, ‘I and the Father are one.’ (John 10:30). They tried to stone him for blasphemy.”

Say: “John’s Gospel has seven ‘I am’ statements: bread of life, light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, truth and life, the true vine. At his trial, the high priest asked, ‘Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?’ Jesus said, ‘I am; and you will see the Son of man seated at the right hand of Power.’ (Mark 14:62) The high priest tore his robes. Jesus was condemned for blasphemy because he claimed to be God. He accepted worship, from Thomas and others, which a faithful Jew would never accept if he were only a man.”

Say: “C. S. Lewis made a famous argument. Jesus said he forgave sins and that he was one with God. ‘A man who was merely a man and said the sort of things Jesus said would not be a great moral teacher. He would either be a lunatic—on the level with the man who says he is a poached egg—or else he would be the Devil of Hell. You must make your choice. Either this man was, and is, the Son of God, or else a madman or something worse.’ This is called the trilemma: Lord, liar or lunatic. Critics say there are other options, like legend. But the Gospels, the Resurrection, and the early Christians’ worship of Jesus as Lord point to the Church’s faith. Thomas’s answer is the right one: ‘My Lord and my God.’”
ask: Name a claim of Jesus that points to divinity. (Forgiving sins; “Before Abraham was, I am”; “I and the Father are one.”)
Why was Jesus condemned? (For blasphemy; he claimed to be the Son of God.)
What is Lewis’s trilemma? (Lord, liar or lunatic.)
practice: List Jesus’ seven “I am” statements with references.
Write what each claims about him.
Mark with a star those that clearly claim divinity.
Write a paragraph answering: “Was Jesus just a good teacher?”
script.close: Pray Thomas’s words together: “My Lord and my God!” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say ‘My Lord and my God’ at the elevation at Mass.”

tryit: List Jesus’ “I am” statements.
Mark which claim divinity.
Explain why Lewis calls the choice Lord, liar or lunatic.
lessons.saintStory:
Thomas, also called Didymus, “the twin,” was one of the Twelve. John’s Gospel tells us the most about him. When Jesus decided to go to Bethany, near Jerusalem, where he had enemies, to raise Lazarus, Thomas said to the others, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” At the Last Supper, when Jesus said, “You know the way where I am going,” Thomas said, “Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?” Jesus answered, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
After the Resurrection, Thomas was not with the others when Jesus appeared. He said, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, and place my finger in the mark of the nails, and place my hand in his side, I will not believe.” A week later, Jesus came again and said, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side; do not be faithless, but believing.” Thomas answered, “My Lord and my God!”
Tradition says Thomas carried the Gospel to India, where he was martyred near Chennai, around AD 72. The Saint Thomas Christians in Kerala trace their faith to him.

lessons.title: Teacher of the kingdom
lessons.idea: Jesus began his ministry proclaiming, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.” His teaching in parables and the Sermon on the Mount reveals the Kingdom and calls for conversion.
lessons.question: What is the kingdom?
lessons.activity: “Analyze three parables” (35 min). Groups study the sower (Mark 4), the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35) and the great banquet (Luke 14:15–24). For each: setting, surprise, what it says about the Kingdom, and a challenge. Create a one-minute dramatization.
teach: The Kingdom of God is the central message (CCC 541–546). It is a gift, grows like a seed, and requires conversion (Mark 1:15). It is already present in Jesus and will come in fullness at the end (CCC 2816).
Parables use everyday images to call hearers to decide (CCC 546). Jesus invites all, “especially the poor and sinners” (CCC 543).
The Sermon on the Mount sets out the Kingdom’s ethic (Matthew 5–7).
The Church is the seed and beginning of the Kingdom on earth (CCC 541, 768).
quiz: The Kingdom of God in Jesus’ preaching is…|God’s reign, present in Christ and still to come in fullness (CCC 541–546)|A philosophy|Only heaven|A political state|0|CCC 541–546.
Parables use ordinary images to…|Entertain|Hide the Gospel|Teach farming|Reveal and challenge, calling hearers to decide (CCC 546)|3|CCC 546.

lessons.life: Interpret three parables with the Catechism.
lessons.saint: Dominic: a preacher who sold his books to feed the hungry and spent his life teaching the truth.
misc: “The Kingdom of God is only in heaven.”
lessons.mem: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.” (Mark 1:15)
lessons.hook: Read Mark 1:14–15. Ask: “What would it mean if a king’s rule were arriving in your town?” Prepare your life.
lessons.assess: Ask students to retell a parable and say what it teaches about the Kingdom.

script.open: Read aloud a short parable, such as the Pearl of Great Price, without saying where it comes from. Ask, “What is the point? Who is it about?” Compare answers before naming the source.
teach: Say: “Jesus began his public ministry by saying: ‘The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent, and believe in the gospel.’ (Mark 1:15) The Kingdom of God is the central theme of his preaching. Jesus is a teacher with authority; the crowds were ‘astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.’ (Mark 1:22) He taught in synagogues, hillsides and boats, and in parables and short sayings. His message: God is a loving Father who seeks the lost; the Kingdom is among us; we must repent, trust and love.”

Say: “The Kingdom is both present and future. It is present in Jesus himself, in his words and works: ‘If it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.’ (Luke 11:20) It is growing in history, like a mustard seed. And it will be fulfilled at the end of time, when Christ returns. The Church is the seed and beginning of the Kingdom on earth. We pray in the Our Father, ‘Thy kingdom come.’ The Kingdom is God’s reign over hearts, a reign of justice, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17).”

Say: “Jesus’ teaching includes: love of God and neighbor as the greatest commandment; the Sermon on the Mount, with the Beatitudes; the call to forgive; humility (‘the last shall be first’); radical trust in the Father (‘Do not be anxious’); and the demand to take up the cross. He spoke of a narrow gate and wide gate, and the Last Judgment. He called people to follow him as disciples, and he formed the Twelve. Notice how he taught: with questions, stories and example. He did not just give information; he called for decision. ‘Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?’ (Luke 6:46)”
ask: What was the center of Jesus’ preaching? (The Kingdom of God.)
Is the Kingdom present or future? (Both.)
How did Jesus teach? (Parables, questions, stories, example, with authority.)
practice: Choose three Kingdom parables: the sower, the mustard seed, the pearl of great price.
Write the main point of each in a sentence.
Write one thing the Kingdom asks of you now.
Share with a partner.
script.close: Pray the Our Father slowly, pausing at “Thy kingdom come.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Choose one teaching of Jesus to live this week.”

tryit: Map the themes of the Kingdom parables.
Write the main point of three.
Say what the Kingdom asks of you.
lessons.saintStory:
Dominic Guzmán was born around 1170 in Castile, Spain. As a student at Palencia, he studied the Bible and theology. During a famine, he sold his books, even those heavily annotated in his own hand, to feed the poor. “Would you have me study from dead skins when men are dying of hunger?” he said.
As a priest, he traveled with his bishop to southern France, where many had embraced the Albigensian heresy, which taught that the material world was evil. He saw that preachers there were wealthy and arrogant, while the heretics lived simply. Dominic decided that the way to reach people was to preach, and to do so in poverty, on foot, with deep learning and example. He founded an order of preachers, the Dominicans, approved in 1216.
He believed in prayer and study, and he sent his friars to the new universities. A tradition holds that Mary gave him the Rosary. He died in 1221. His motto: to praise, to bless, to preach.

lessons.title: Signs and miracles
lessons.idea: Jesus’ miracles are signs that the Kingdom has come. They show his power over nature, sin, sickness and death, and invite faith. Skeptics such as Hume argue against miracles; Christians respond that if God exists, miracles are possible and testimony can establish them.
lessons.question: Are miracles credible?
lessons.activity: “Respond to a skeptic” (35 min). Students respond to Hume’s argument (“a miracle is a violation of laws of nature, and testimony is never enough”). In pairs, they draft a short reply: laws describe regular causes, not what God can do; testimony can be strong; probability must consider the evidence. Debate.
teach: Miracles accompany Jesus’ word and show the Kingdom has begun (CCC 547–550). They are “signs” of his identity, not tricks (CCC 548).
Faith is the response; Jesus often asks for it before a healing (Mark 5:34). Miracles do not force belief (John 12:37).
Philosophically, if God exists he can act in the world (CCC 156). Hume’s argument has been criticized as circular. Lourdes and Church-investigated healings continue (CCC 2003).
The greatest miracle is the Resurrection (CCC 647).
quiz: A “sign” in John’s Gospel is…|A work that points beyond itself to who Jesus is (John 2:11)|A prophecy|A magic trick|A hallucination|0|John 2:11.

Hume’s argument against miracles has been criticized because it…|Is certainly right|Is scientific|Uses Scripture|Assumes in advance that miracles do not occur, so no testimony could be enough|3|Common critique.
Which best describes the purpose of Jesus’ miracles?|To manifest the Kingdom and invite faith (CCC 547–550)|To cause fear|To show off|To pay debts|0|CCC 547–550.
lessons.life: Read a modern, approved miracle account (Lourdes).
lessons.saint: Bartimaeus: the blind beggar who shouted until Jesus stopped.
lessons.mem: “This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.” (John 2:11)
lessons.hook: Read John 2:11 (“the first of his signs”). Ask: “A sign points to something. What does the wedding wine point to?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what a sign is and answer one objection.

script.open: Display a list of ten possible reactions to seeing a miracle: awe, doubt, fear, joy, denial. Ask students to rank how they would likely react, and why. Use the ranking to read Mark 5.
teach: Say: “The Gospels record about thirty-five miracles, and say Jesus did many more (John 21:25). They are of four kinds: healings of sickness and disability, exorcisms, nature miracles, and raising the dead. Jesus’ miracles are called ‘signs’ and ‘mighty works.’ They show that the Kingdom has come. They reveal his identity and compassion. He healed lepers, who were outcasts, and he touched them. Many occurred in response to faith: ‘Your faith has made you well.’ At Nazareth, ‘he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.’ (Matthew 13:58)”

Say: “A miracle is an event that goes beyond the natural order and is caused by God, a sign to those who see. A natural explanation isn’t always possible. The Church takes miracles seriously and tests them. David Hume argued that miracles are impossible because the evidence of experience is against them. But this assumes the answer. If God exists, miracles are possible. The question is whether the evidence for a particular miracle is good. For the Gospels, the Resurrection is the central miracle. The Church today investigates healings, such as those at Lourdes, with medical panels. Of thousands of claimed cures, only about seventy are recognized as miraculous.”

Say: “What is the point of a miracle? They are not mere displays of power. Jesus refused to turn stones into bread or jump from the Temple. They point to who he is and call for faith. They show God’s concern for the whole person, body and soul. In John’s Gospel, the signs lead to a discourse: the feeding of the five thousand leads to the Bread of Life; healing of the blind man leads to ‘I am the light of the world’; the raising of Lazarus leads to ‘I am the resurrection and the life.’ Miracles are also signs of the sacraments: Jesus’ healing touch continues in Anointing, his forgiveness in Penance. The greatest miracle is the conversion of a heart.”
ask: What are four kinds of miracles? (Healings, exorcisms, nature, raising the dead.)
Why did Jesus work miracles? (To show the Kingdom and reveal who he is, and from compassion.)
Why did he not do many at Nazareth? (Unbelief.)
practice: Make a chart: Miracle, Type, What it reveals about Jesus, What it asks of us.
Pick the one that speaks to you most.
Write a short reply to a friend who says miracles are impossible.
script.close: Pray Bartimaeus’s prayer: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say the Jesus Prayer five times a day.”

tryit: Classify the miracles in a chart.
Write what each sign reveals.
Respond to a skeptic.
lessons.saintStory:
Bartimaeus, “son of Timaeus,” was a blind beggar who sat by the roadside outside Jericho. When he heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing, he began to shout, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Many in the crowd told him to be quiet. He cried out all the louder.
Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” They said to the blind man, “Take heart; rise, he is calling you.” Bartimaeus threw off his cloak, probably his only possession, sprang up and came to Jesus. Jesus asked, “What do you want me to do for you?” He said, “Master, let me receive my sight.” Jesus said, “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus on the way.
Mark remembers his name, which suggests he became a known member of the early Church. He is a model of persistent prayer and of faith.

lessons.title: Why did Jesus come?
lessons.idea: Why did the Son of God become man? To save us by reconciling us to God, to show us God’s love, to be our model of holiness and to make us “partakers of the divine nature.” The Church Fathers: “God became man so that man might become God.”
lessons.question: What does he save us from?
lessons.activity: “Four reasons” statement (25 min). Students write a statement answering “Why did Jesus come?” in four parts, with a verse for each (John 3:16; 1 John 4:9–10; John 13:15; 2 Peter 1:4). Share and compare.
teach: CCC 456–460 gives four reasons: to save us by reconciling us with God, to show us God’s love, to be our model of holiness, and to make us “partakers of the divine nature.”
Athanasius: “The Son of God became man so that we might become God” (CCC 460) — meaning sharing in God’s life by grace, not becoming God by nature.
The Incarnation is the center of the whole plan of redemption. The New Testament uses many images: ransom, reconciliation, adoption.
Link to the Christmas season and to Easter: one mystery.
quiz: Which is NOT one of the four reasons the Word became flesh (CCC 457–460)?|To abolish the Old Testament|To show us God’s love|To be our model of holiness|To save us by reconciling us with God|0|CCC 457–460.
Athanasius’ line “God became man that man might become god” means…|Humans are divine|We become God by nature|We share by grace in God’s life (CCC 460)|Nothing|2|CCC 460.
John 3:16 stresses that the Incarnation arises from…|Human merit|Necessity|Fate|God’s love|3|John 3:16.
lessons.life: Write your own summary of why Jesus came.
lessons.saint: Gregory of Nazianzus: a bishop and poet who said that what Christ did not take on, he did not heal.
misc: “Jesus came only to teach a moral code.”
lessons.mem: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:16)
lessons.hook: Read John 3:16. Ask: “What would you do for someone you love? What did God do?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to give the four reasons for the Incarnation with a verse each.

script.open: Ask, “If you were drowning and someone could save you by jumping in, but couldn’t swim, would they save you? What would a rescuer need?” Take answers. “Let’s see what Jesus needed to be for us.”
teach: Say: “Why did the Son of God become man? The Catechism gives four reasons (CCC 457-460). One: to save us by reconciling us with God. The Creed says, ‘For us men and for our salvation he came down from heaven.’ ‘God loved us and sent his Son to be the expiation for our sins.’ (1 John 4:10) Two: that we might know God’s love: ‘God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.’ (John 3:16) Three: to be our model of holiness: ‘Learn from me; for I am gentle and lowly in heart.’ (Matthew 11:29) Four: to make us partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). ‘The Son of God became man so that we might become God.’”

Say: “Gregory’s principle explains why the human nature was needed: if Christ did not assume all of human nature, including a human mind and will, then the parts he did not assume were not redeemed. He took on human flesh, mind and soul, to heal all of it. Only God can save us, and only a man can die. Anselm asked in Cur Deus Homo: why did God become man? Because sin offends God infinitely, and humanity owes a debt that humans can’t pay; only God could; but a human must. The God-man pays the debt out of love.”

Say: “Notice also that Jesus came for a mission: to proclaim the Kingdom, to call sinners (‘I came not to call the righteous, but sinners’), to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), to give life abundantly (John 10:10), to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37), and to establish the Church. There are different theories of the atonement: some stress ransom (we were captives), some satisfaction (a debt), some victory (over sin, death and Satan), some example. The Church holds them together. Salvation means freedom from sin and death, reconciliation with God, adoption as children and the gift of eternal life.”
ask: What are four reasons for the Incarnation? (To save us, show God’s love, be our model, share his divine life.)
What did Gregory teach about Christ’s humanity? (What he did not assume, he did not heal.)
Which verse says Jesus gave his life as a ransom? (Mark 10:45.)
practice: Make a four-column chart: reason, verse, what it means, what difference it makes to me.
Fill in each from the Catechism.
Choose the reason that speaks most to you and write a short paragraph.
Share it in a small group.
script.close: Pray: “Lord Jesus, you came down for us and for our salvation. Thank you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank Jesus for one reason in particular.”

tryit: List the reasons the Catechism gives for the Incarnation.
Match each with a verse.
Say which matters most to you.
lessons.saintStory:
Gregory was born around 329 in Cappadocia, in what is now Turkey. His father was a bishop. He studied in Athens, where he met Basil, and the two became close friends. Gregory wanted a quiet life of study and prayer, but the Church kept calling him out of it. His father pressured him to be ordained a priest; he fled, then returned. Basil made him bishop of a small village that Gregory hated.
In 379, the small group of orthodox Christians in Constantinople, where Arians dominated, asked him to lead them. He gave brilliant sermons in a small chapel, his “Theological Orations,” which defended the Trinity and the divinity of Christ. He was made bishop of Constantinople, but disliked the politics, and resigned during the Council of 381.
He retired to his family estate and wrote poetry and letters. He died around 390. He is called “the Theologian.” In one letter he wrote: “That which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.”

units.title: The Paschal Mystery
units.eq: What happened on Calvary and Easter?

lessons.title: Why did Jesus die?
lessons.idea: Jesus died for our sins, in accordance with the Scriptures, as a sacrifice freely offered out of love. The New Testament and the Church use several images — ransom, sacrifice, satisfaction, expiation — none of which exhausts the mystery.
lessons.question: What does “atonement” mean?
lessons.activity: “Compare theories of atonement” (35 min). Students compare: ransom (Origen), satisfaction (Anselm), penal substitution, moral influence (Abelard), Christus Victor. For each: the idea, a verse, a strength and a weakness. The Church has not defined one theory; the Catechism uses several (CCC 615–618).
teach: Christ died “for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3; CCC 599–605). His death fulfills Isaiah 53 and was freely accepted (CCC 609–614).

The Church does not teach that the Father is a cruel judge who punishes an innocent victim. The Father gives his Son; the Son freely offers himself; it is one act of love of the Trinity (CCC 603–605).
Images: redemption (a price paid), sacrifice, expiation, reconciliation (CCC 615–618). The Cross makes possible our salvation and is renewed in the Mass.
Handle “penal substitution” carefully; Catholic teaching emphasizes love and satisfaction rather than a punishment transferred.
talk: What does it demand of us?
quiz: Which model of the Cross appears in Mark 10:45?|Exchange|Magic|Moral example only|Ransom|3|Mark 10:45.

The Catholic Church does not teach that…|Christ’s death is a sacrifice of love|The Father is cruel and demands a victim; the Father and Son act in one love (CCC 603–605)|Christ freely gave himself|Sin has consequences|1|CCC 603–605.
Christus Victor emphasizes…|Christ’s victory over sin and death|Nothing|Moral influence only|Satisfaction only|0|One image among several.
lessons.life: Contemplate the Cross for 10 minutes.
lessons.saint: Dismas: the thief on the cross who asked to be remembered.
misc: “Jesus’ death was only a moral example.”
lessons.mem: “For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45)
lessons.hook: Show an object and ask: “What is the cost of love?” A parent’s sacrifice. Look at Mark 10:45: “to give his life as a ransom for many.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe two models of atonement and avoid a common distortion.

script.open: Be serious. Say, “Today we deal with the central event of Christianity. We’ll be honest about it. Why did Jesus die? Who killed him?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Jesus was arrested after the Last Supper, tried before the Sanhedrin, and handed to Pilate, who ordered his crucifixion. The Romans carried out the crucifixion, a brutal and shameful punishment for rebels and slaves. Historians agree that this happened; even Tacitus mentions it. But why? On the human level, some of the religious leaders feared him, Pilate feared unrest, Judas betrayed him, Peter denied him, and the crowd shouted. The Church teaches that Jesus’ death cannot be attributed to the Jewish people as a whole, then or now. Vatican II’s Nostra Aetate says so clearly: ‘What happened in his passion cannot be blamed upon all the Jews then living, without distinction, nor upon the Jews of today.’”

Say: “On the deeper level, the Catechism says that sinners were the authors and agents of the Passion. ‘We must regard as guilty all those who continue to relapse into their sins.’ (CCC 598) Our sins nailed him to the cross. But Jesus freely gave himself: ‘No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.’ (John 10:18) He said at the Last Supper that his body is given for us. The Father did not will the evil that killed his Son, but he willed that the Son would give himself in love. The cross is a sacrifice: Jesus is both priest and victim. It reveals God’s love: ‘Greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.’ (John 15:13)”

Say: “How does his death save us? The Letter to the Hebrews describes Christ as the high priest who offers himself once for all. Isaiah 53 says the suffering servant bears our iniquities. Jesus said at the Last Supper, ‘my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.’ (Matthew 26:28) The Church calls this redemption (buying back), reconciliation (restoring friendship), expiation (taking away sin), and sacrifice. Nobody could fully explain, but we trust. The crucifix is central to Catholic life because it shows God’s love for us. It is not defeat but victory: ‘By his wounds we are healed.’”
ask: Who is responsible for Jesus’ death? (All sinners; not the Jewish people as a whole.)
What did Jesus say of his life? (No one takes it; I lay it down of my own accord.)
What does the Catechism say sinners did? (They were the authors and agents of the Passion.)
practice: Read Mark 15:21-39 and Luke 23:33-49 side by side.
Make a chart: who was there, what each did, what they said.
Mark where there are signs of faith or mercy.
Write a reflection: “At the cross, I stand with…”
script.close: Pray Dismas’s prayer: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray before a crucifix tonight.”

tryit: Read the accounts of the Passion side by side.
List who was responsible.
Explain what the Church teaches about guilt.
lessons.saintStory:
Luke tells us that two criminals were crucified with Jesus, one on his right and one on his left. One of them mocked him: “Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!” The other rebuked him: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? And we indeed justly; for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.” Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come in your kingly power.”
Jesus said to him, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise.” This is the only person in the Gospels whom Jesus promises Paradise directly.
The name Dismas comes from later tradition. He is the patron saint of prisoners and the dying. His story shows the heart of Good Friday: even at the last minute, a sincere prayer for mercy is heard. At the same time, he did not delay till the last minute by plan; no one knows the hour.

lessons.title: The Resurrection
lessons.idea: Jesus rose bodily on the third day. It is both a historical event and a transcendent mystery. The evidence — the empty tomb, the appearances to many people, and the transformation of the disciples — led to the Church’s faith.
lessons.question: How strong is the evidence?
lessons.activity: “Weigh the evidence” debate (40 min). Teams argue for and against the proposition “The best explanation of the evidence is that Jesus rose from the dead.” Teams use 1 Corinthians 15:3–8, Luke 24, the empty tomb, the appearances, the disciples’ transformation, and alternatives (hallucination, theft, swoon, myth). Conclude with the Church’s claim.
teach: The Resurrection is a historical event attested by signs and also transcends history (CCC 639–647). Paul lists witnesses, including more than 500 at once, most still alive (1 Corinthians 15:3–8).
Alternatives struggle: hallucinations don’t explain group appearances or the empty tomb; theft doesn’t explain the transformation; swoon theory fails given Roman execution.
The first witnesses were women, an unlikely invention in that culture. The disciples were willing to die for it.
The Resurrection invites faith; it is not coercive proof (CCC 644). It is the foundation of Christian hope (CCC 651–655).
talk: What does it mean for us?
quiz: Which line of evidence is strongest for the first witnesses being sincere?|They hid|They gained wealth|They died for what they proclaimed|They were soldiers|2|Martyrdom of apostles.

The first witnesses being women is significant because…|It was typical|In that culture women’s testimony counted little, so it is unlikely to be invented|They were not present|It does not matter|1|Matthew 28; John 20.
The Resurrection is both…|Historical and transcendent (CCC 639–647)|Only legend|Only spiritual|Only symbolic|0|CCC 639–647.
lessons.life: Read 1 Corinthians 15 aloud.
lessons.saint: Joseph of Arimathea: a secret disciple who found the courage to ask Pilate for the body.
misc: “The Resurrection was only a spiritual experience.”
lessons.mem: “If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.” (1 Corinthians 15:14)
lessons.hook: Say: “If you wanted to prove a big claim in court, you would want witnesses, physical evidence, and motive.” Apply to the Resurrection.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present evidence for the Resurrection and respond to one alternative.

script.open: Say, “Imagine the day after Good Friday. Jesus is dead. His followers are scattered. What do you think happens next, by normal expectations? Would the movement continue?” Take answers.
teach: Read Matthew 28:1-10 and 1 Corinthians 15:3-8. Say: “The Resurrection is the central event of the Christian faith. The earliest creed, in Paul, written around AD 55 but handed on from earlier, says that Jesus died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Peter, the Twelve, more than 500 at once, James and Paul. The Gospels say the tomb was found empty by women on Sunday morning. The women were the first witnesses, which an invented story in that culture would probably not use, since women’s testimony was not accepted as legal evidence.”

Say: “What explanations are there? The disciples stole the body: but they would not die for something they knew was a lie. The authorities moved it: they would have produced the body to stop the movement. The women went to the wrong tomb: Joseph’s tomb was well known. Jesus did not really die (swoon theory): the Romans were experts, and he was pierced with a spear. The apostles hallucinated: hallucinations are individual, not shared by groups, and do not explain the empty tomb. A legend developed: the creed in 1 Corinthians 15 comes within a few years. The simplest explanation is what the apostles said: he rose.”

Say: “The Church teaches that the Resurrection is a real event in history, and also transcends history. Jesus was not resuscitated, like Lazarus, but rose with a glorified body, unlimited by space and death. He could appear in locked rooms, yet showed his wounds and ate fish. The resurrection is the foundation: ‘If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain.’ It confirms his divinity, shows God accepted his sacrifice, defeats death, and is the source of our own resurrection and justification (Romans 4:25). We celebrate it every Sunday and especially at Easter. Faith in it is a gift, but the evidence is substantial.”
ask: What are some alternative explanations for the empty tomb? (Stolen body, wrong tomb, swoon, hallucination, legend.)
Why are women as first witnesses significant? (An invented story would not use them in that culture.)
How is Jesus’ resurrection different from Lazarus’s? (He rose to a glorified life; Lazarus returned to ordinary life and died again.)
practice: Make a table: Explanation, Evidence for, Problems with it.
Include six explanations.
Rate each: very plausible, plausible, unlikely.
Write a paragraph on which explanation best fits all the facts.
script.close: Pray: “Christ is risen! He is risen indeed!” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 aloud.”

tryit: Weigh the explanations for the empty tomb.
Test each against the evidence.
State the Church’s claim.
lessons.saintStory:
Joseph of Arimathea was a rich man and a member of the council, the Sanhedrin, who had not consented to the plan to condemn Jesus. John says he was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews. After Jesus died, Joseph went boldly to Pilate and asked for the body. Pilate checked that Jesus was already dead and gave permission.
With Nicodemus, who brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes, he took the body down, wrapped it in linen cloths with spices, according to Jewish burial custom, and laid it in his own new tomb, cut in rock, where no one had yet been laid. They rolled a large stone across the entrance. It was late on Friday, just before the Sabbath began.
His courage came at the moment when the Twelve had fled. By giving Jesus a proper burial, he became an unexpected witness: the tomb was known. Everyone could later check where the body had been placed.

lessons.title: Ascension and Parousia
lessons.idea: Jesus ascended to the Father and sits at his right hand; he will return in glory at the Parousia to judge the living and the dead. Until then, he is present in his Church and the sacraments, and we live in hopeful expectation.
lessons.question: What does it mean?
lessons.activity: “Creed commentary” (30 min). Students write a short commentary on the lines “He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father; he will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead.” Define each phrase and say how it affects daily life.
teach: The Ascension is Christ’s enthronement in glory and our hope to follow (CCC 659–667). “The right hand of the Father” means authority and honor.
The Parousia, the second coming, will bring final judgment and the fullness of the Kingdom (CCC 668–679). No one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36).
In the meantime, the Church lives between Christ’s first and second comings (CCC 671–672).
Resist speculation about dates, as Jesus warns.

The Parousia is…|His birth|A feast|His baptism|The Second Coming of Christ in glory (CCC 668–679)|3|CCC 668–679.
Jesus teaches about the day of his return that…|No one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36)|It is next year|It is yesterday|It is calculable|0|Matthew 24:36.
lessons.life: Write a creed paragraph on the Ascension.
lessons.saint: Vincent Ferrer: a preacher who warned of the Last Judgment and brought people to repentance.
misc: “We can calculate the date of the Second Coming.”
lessons.mem: “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” (Acts 1:11)
lessons.hook: Read Acts 1:9–11. Ask: “Why did the angels ask, ‘Why do you stand looking into heaven?’” We are meant to act while we wait.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Ascension and the Parousia and how they shape Christian life.

script.open: Show the final scene of Jesus’ Ascension in a painting, and ask students to describe the faces of the disciples. Say, “Are they sad, hopeful, afraid? Why?” Take observations.
teach: Read Acts 1:6-11. Say: “Forty days after the Resurrection, Jesus ascended into heaven. This means that Jesus, in his glorified human body, returned to the Father, to be our advocate. He sits at the right hand of the Father, a sign of authority. He is not absent: ‘I am with you always.’ (Matthew 28:20) He intercedes for us (Hebrews 7:25), prepares a place for us (John 14:2), and sends the Spirit. The angels said, ‘This Jesus… will come in the same way as you saw him go.’”

Say: “The Second Coming of Christ is called the Parousia, Greek for ‘presence’ or ‘arrival.’ The Creed says, ‘He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.’ When? ‘Of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.’ (Mark 13:32) The Church warns against predicting dates. Before the end, the Church must go through a final trial (CCC 675), but we don’t know the details. The Church prays ‘Marana tha,’ ‘Come, Lord.’ Every Mass says it: ‘We proclaim your death, O Lord, and profess your Resurrection until you come again.’”

Say: “The Church teaches that there are two judgments. The particular judgment: at death, each soul is judged and goes to heaven, purgatory or hell. The general or Last Judgment: at the end of time, Christ will come, the dead will be raised, and the whole truth of each life will be revealed. Matthew 25:31-46: we will be judged on love for the least of his brothers. This is not meant to frighten but to motivate. The resurrection of the body: at the end, our bodies will be raised, glorified. And there will be new heavens and a new earth. Vigilance means living now in a way that welcomes Christ. Jesus said, ‘Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.’”
ask: What does the Ascension mean? (Jesus returned to the Father in his glorified humanity.)
What is the Parousia? (Christ’s Second Coming.)
What are the two judgments? (Particular at death; general at the end.)
practice: Make a timeline: Ascension, the Church’s age, the final trial, the Parousia, the resurrection of the dead, the Last Judgment, new heavens and earth.
Mark the parts the Bible clearly states and those it does not.
Read Matthew 25:31-46 and list the questions the Judge asks.
Write three habits of living ready.
script.close: Pray: “Come, Lord Jesus.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one of the works of mercy from Matthew 25 this week.”

tryit: Lay out the end-times events in order.
Mark what Scripture says and what it does not.
Write what living ready looks like.
lessons.saintStory:
Vincent Ferrer was born in Valencia, Spain, around 1350. He became a Dominican, and was a brilliant professor. In 1398, during a serious illness in Avignon, he said that Jesus, with Dominic and Francis, appeared to him and told him to go out and preach repentance. He recovered and spent the next twenty years traveling on foot and by donkey throughout Spain, France, Italy and the Low Countries, preaching to huge crowds. He spoke in Catalan, and yet people of other languages claimed to understand him.
His theme: “Fear God and give him glory, for the hour of his judgment has come.” His sermons called people to repent, to forgive their enemies and to prepare for death. Thousands of sinners were reconciled. He also worked to end the Western Schism, when there were rival claimants to the papacy, and he supported a council that ended it.
He died in 1419 in Vannes. He is patron of builders and of Valencia. He taught that to prepare for the Judgment means to love now.

lessons.title: Faith and discipleship
lessons.idea: Following Jesus means denying ourselves, taking up the cross daily and following him. Discipleship is a response to a call, a relationship and a way of life. The call stories show how Jesus invites ordinary people.
lessons.question: What does it cost?
lessons.activity: “Call story reflection” (30 min). Students read three call stories (Matthew 4:18–22, Luke 5:1–11, John 1:35–51). They note what Jesus does, the response, the cost. Then write about a moment they sensed an invitation from God.
teach: Christian life is following Christ (CCC 520, 1694). “If any man would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me” (Luke 9:23).
All are called to holiness (CCC 2013–2015). The call comes from God’s initiative and requires our free response (CCC 1812–1829).
The cross is not self-hatred but self-giving love. The Beatitudes show the path (CCC 1716–1724).
Discipleship is lived in community, the Church, with the sacraments and prayer.
quiz: Luke 9:23 calls disciples to…|Deny themselves, take up the cross daily and follow|Obey law only|Comfort|Leave society|0|Luke 9:23.
The cross in the Christian life is…|Self-hatred|Seeking pain|A symbol only|Self-giving love united to Christ (CCC 618)|3|CCC 618.
All are called to…|Only marriage|Only priesthood|Holiness (CCC 2013)|Nothing|2|CCC 2013.
lessons.life: Choose one cross to carry this week.
lessons.saint: Andrew Kim Taegon: Korea’s first native priest, who died at twenty-five for the faith his people had started on their own.
misc: “Taking up the cross means seeking suffering.”
lessons.mem: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.” (Luke 9:23)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 9:23. Ask: “What does ‘take up your cross daily’ look like for a teenager?” Honest answers.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what discipleship asks and give a concrete example.

script.open: Write on the board, ‘Follow me.’ Ask, “What is the difference between agreeing with someone and following them?” Take three answers, then read how the first disciples responded.
teach: Say: “The Gospel of Mark has a clear structure about discipleship. Jesus calls: ‘Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.’ (Mark 1:17) The first disciples left their nets at once. He appoints the Twelve ‘to be with him, and to be sent out.’ He teaches and shows them signs. At Caesarea Philippi, Peter says, ‘You are the Christ.’ Immediately Jesus teaches them that the Son of Man must suffer, and Peter rebukes him. Jesus says, ‘Get behind me, Satan.’ Then he gives the cost: ‘If any man would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.’ (Mark 8:34)”

Say: “Discipleship is a relationship before it’s a rule. It begins with a call, a response, and a life lived with Jesus. The disciples were slow to understand, they argued about who was greatest, they fell asleep in Gethsemane, they fled, and Peter denied him. Yet Jesus did not give up on them. After the Resurrection, he restored Peter. Discipleship is about conversion, which is lifelong. Faith is an act of the whole person: the mind accepts, the will chooses, the heart loves, and it shows in life. James writes, ‘Faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead.’”

Say: “What does it cost? Jesus is clear: the rich young man went away sad because he had many possessions. ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.’ We are asked to put Jesus first, to take up our cross daily, to forgive, to serve. It also gives much: ‘Everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters… for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and inherit eternal life.’ (Matthew 19:29) Discipleship is lived in the Church, with others. The vocation of the baptized is to be missionary disciples. Each of us can ask: What is Jesus calling me to now?”
ask: What did Jesus say is the cost of discipleship? (Deny yourself, take up your cross and follow him.)
How did the disciples respond to Jesus’ suffering? (They struggled, fled, and later returned.)
What does the Church ask of disciples? (Faith lived out in love.)
practice: Make a chart: Call, Response, Cost, Reward.
Write your own “yes” to Jesus: one specific thing you will do this month to follow him more closely.
Share it with a partner for accountability.
script.close: Pray the prayer of discipleship: “Lord, I want to follow you. Show me the way.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Take one small step toward Jesus each day.”

tryit: Trace the steps of discipleship in Mark.
Mark the costs.
Write your own “yes.”
lessons.saintStory:
Korea’s Church began without missionaries. In 1784, a young scholar, Yi Seung-hun, was baptized in Beijing and returned to Korea, where he started to baptize others. The small community of lay people grew for decades before any priest arrived. They suffered severe persecution.
Andrew Kim Taegon was born in 1821 into a Christian family; his great-grandfather and father were both martyred. At fifteen, he was sent to Macau to train for the priesthood, and was ordained in Shanghai in 1845, the first Korean priest. He returned secretly to Korea by sea, and ministered to Christians. In 1846, he was arrested while trying to bring in more missionaries.
In prison he wrote letters encouraging the faithful. He was tortured and beheaded on September 16, 1846, at twenty-five. He is one of 103 Korean martyrs canonized in 1984. A Korean Church that began with lay people has grown into one of the largest in Asia.

lessons.title: Grace and justification
lessons.idea: We are justified by grace through faith, not by our own works. Grace is a free gift of God’s life that forgives sin, makes us holy and enables good works. We cooperate with grace, and God rewards what he himself accomplishes in us.
lessons.question: What is grace?
lessons.activity: “Clear up misunderstandings” (35 min). Students sort statements: “Catholics think they earn salvation” (false), “Faith alone with no response” (not Catholic), “Grace first, faith responds, works flow” (Catholic). Read Ephesians 2:8–10 and James 2:24 and harmonize. Write a two-sentence explanation of justification.
teach: Justification is “the most excellent work of God’s love” (CCC 1994). It is granted in Baptism and takes away sin and makes us sharers in divine life (CCC 1987–1995).

Grace is a free, undeserved gift (CCC 1996–2005). We cannot merit the first grace; afterwards we merit rewards by grace (CCC 2006–2011). “It is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

Ephesians 2:8–10: “by grace you have been saved through faith… for good works.” James 2:24 stresses that faith is alive through works. The Joint Declaration on Justification (1999) with Lutherans shows common ground.
Emphasize hope and humility: salvation is gift and response.
talk: How do faith and works relate?
quiz: Which statement is Catholic?|Faith has no effect|Justification is God’s free gift by grace, received through faith that works in love (CCC 1987–1995; Galatians 5:6)|Once saved always saved|We are saved by works alone|1|CCC 1987–1995.
Merit in Catholic teaching rests on…|Luck|Our own power|God’s grace enabling our good acts (CCC 2006–2011)|Law|2|CCC 2006–2011.
The 1999 Joint Declaration on Justification was between…|Catholics and Lutherans|Anglicans and Methodists|Catholics and Orthodox|Jews and Christians|0|1999.
lessons.life: Pray the Act of Contrition with attention to grace.
lessons.saint: Matt Talbot: a Dublin laborer who found grace in the freedom from alcohol.
lessons.mem: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” (Ephesians 2:8)
lessons.hook: Say: “A gift cannot be earned. But you can open it or leave it on the table.” Grace is like that.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Catholic view of grace, faith and works.

script.open: Ask, “Can a person lift themselves out of a deep pit by pulling on their own hair? What do they need?” Take answers. “That’s a question about grace.”
teach: Say: “Grace is the free and undeserved help that God gives us to respond to his call, to become his children, and to share in his life. The Catechism defines it as ‘favor, the free and undeserved help that God gives us.’ (CCC 1996) We cannot earn it. Paul wrote, ‘For by grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not your own doing, it is the gift of God.’ (Ephesians 2:8) Sanctifying grace is a permanent disposition that makes us holy and friends of God. Actual grace is a particular help in a moment. Sacramental grace is given by each sacrament.”

Say: “Justification is God’s work of making us righteous. It is the beginning of our conversion. In Baptism, God forgives our sins and makes us his children. The Council of Trent taught that justification is not only the forgiveness of sins but the sanctification and renewal of the interior man. It comes from God’s grace, received through faith and the sacraments, and it makes us truly just. We cooperate: grace doesn’t override freedom. We can say yes or no. ‘God, who created you without you, will not save you without you,’ said Augustine.”

Say: “Catholics and Protestants have disagreed about justification. Luther taught that we are justified by faith alone and that righteousness is credited to us from outside. The Catholic Church teaches that faith is the beginning, and that love and good works are fruits of grace. Paul wrote that ‘a man is justified by faith apart from works of law’ (Romans 3:28), meaning works done without Christ, and James wrote that ‘a man is justified by works and not by faith alone’ (James 2:24). We can’t merit the first grace. After that, God’s grace enables us to do works that are meritorious because they are God’s gift. The 1999 Catholic-Lutheran Joint Declaration said we share a basic consensus: ‘By grace alone, in faith in Christ’s saving work… we are accepted by God.’”
ask: What is grace? (God’s free and undeserved help.)
Can we earn the first grace? (No; it is a gift.)
Does grace remove freedom? (No; we cooperate.)
practice: Draw two columns: “What God does” and “What I do.”
Fill in, from Ephesians 2:8-10, James 2:14-26 and the lesson.
Write a short true or imagined story of a change (like Matt Talbot’s), marking where grace came and where a choice was made.
Share with a partner.
script.close: Pray: “By your grace, Lord, I am what I am.” (1 Corinthians 15:10.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank God for a grace you have received.”

tryit: Define grace in your own words.
Mark what God does and what we do.
Write the story of a change.
lessons.saintStory:
Matt Talbot was born in 1856 in Dublin, one of twelve children in a poor family. He left school early, and started work at twelve in a wine merchant’s store. By then he had already started drinking. He drank heavily for sixteen years, spending his wages and even pawning his boots and clothes. His days were a blur.
In 1884, after a weekend with no money, he stood outside a pub waiting for friends to invite him in. No one did. He went home, and told his mother he would take “the pledge.” He took it for three months, and then for life. The first months were hard; he went to Mass every morning, prayed constantly and fell on his knees to ask for help when the temptation came.
He worked as a laborer for the rest of his life, gave much of his money to the poor, and lived simply, praying and fasting. He died on his way to Mass in 1925. Many who struggle with addiction pray to him.

lessons.title: Prayer with the Gospels
lessons.idea: We can pray with the Gospels by entering the scene, meeting Jesus and speaking with him. Lectio divina (read, meditate, pray, contemplate) and Ignatian contemplation (imagining the scene with the senses) are two ancient methods.
lessons.question: How do we encounter Christ?
lessons.activity: “Lectio divina” (35 min). Guide the class through lectio on Luke 24:13–35 in four movements: read and notice a word; meditate; pray a response; rest. Then try an Ignatian imagination exercise: place yourself in the scene as a disciple. Journal.
teach: Lectio divina: lectio (read), meditatio (meditate), oratio (pray), contemplatio (rest) (CCC 2705–2708). The practice is rooted in the Fathers and monasteries.
Ignatian contemplation uses imagination: see, hear, touch the scene and speak with Jesus (CCC 2708, 2715). Jesus is the one who “looks at us”.
The Jesus Prayer anchors attention (CCC 2616). Gospel prayer should lead to action.
Suggest students pray with the Sunday Gospel during the week.
quiz: Lectio divina has movements of…|Ask, seek, knock|Tell, listen, vote|Sing, dance, fast|Read, meditate, pray, contemplate|3|CCC 2705–2708.
Ignatian contemplation uses…|Statistics|Imagination to enter a Gospel scene and speak with Christ|Silence only|Memorization|1|Spiritual Exercises.
The Emmaus story shows Jesus…|Teaching nothing|Explaining Scripture and being known in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:13–35)|Leaving|Hiding|1|Luke 24.
lessons.life: Do lectio divina every day this week with one Gospel scene.
lessons.saint: Mary: the mother who pondered everything in her heart.
misc: “Imagination in prayer is making things up.”
lessons.mem: “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road?” (Luke 24:32)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 24:13–35 slowly. Ask: “If you were walking beside Jesus on the road to Emmaus, what would you say?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to practice a brief lectio and explain the four movements.

script.open: Give each person a short Gospel passage on a slip. Ask them to read it twice silently and to underline one word. Go around and have each person read just that word aloud, to hear what the group notices.
teach: Say: “The Gospels are not just stories from the past; they are living words. The Church has many ways to pray with Scripture. Lectio divina, ‘sacred reading,’ has four steps: lectio (read the passage slowly), meditatio (reflect on what it says), oratio (respond to God in prayer) and contemplatio (rest in God’s presence). Ignatius of Loyola taught another way: Gospel contemplation, imagining yourself in a scene. See the people, hear the words, feel what happens. Ask what Jesus says to you. This is not make-believe; it engages our mind and heart with God’s word.”

Say: “Here’s how to do it. First, pray for the Spirit. Second, read the passage slowly, and read it a second time. Third, imagine the scene: What does the place look like? Who is there? What are they feeling? Put yourself in the scene, perhaps as a bystander or as one of the characters. Fourth, notice what Jesus says and does. How does he look at you? Fifth, speak to him as to a friend: tell him what you feel, ask for what you need, thank him. Sixth, close with an Our Father, and note what stood out. You may find yourself surprised. Write it in a journal.”

Say: “The Gospels also help us pray the Rosary, which Pope John Paul II called ‘a compendium of the Gospel.’ In the Rosary, we meditate on twenty mysteries: Joyful (Annunciation, Visitation, Nativity, Presentation, Finding in the Temple), Luminous (Baptism, Cana, Proclamation of the Kingdom, Transfiguration, Eucharist), Sorrowful (Agony, Scourging, Crowning with Thorns, Carrying the Cross, Crucifixion) and Glorious (Resurrection, Ascension, Descent of the Spirit, Assumption, Coronation). While the lips say the Hail Mary, the mind contemplates the scene with Mary. Regular prayer with Scripture is one of the best ways to get to know Jesus. He is not just a figure in a book but is present and speaks.”
ask: What are the four steps of lectio divina? (Read, meditate, pray, contemplate.)
How do you pray with imagination? (Picture the scene, place yourself in it, speak with Jesus.)
What are the four sets of Rosary mysteries? (Joyful, Luminous, Sorrowful, Glorious.)
practice: Choose a short Gospel passage such as Mark 10:46-52 or Luke 19:1-10.
Pray it using the six steps in silence for ten minutes.
Write what you saw, what Jesus said, and what you answered.
Share a small part with a partner if you wish.
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary with the mystery of the Visitation in mind. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Spend ten minutes praying with a Gospel scene.”

tryit: Pray a Gospel scene using imagination.
Write what you saw, heard and said.
End with a conversation with Jesus.
lessons.saintStory:
Luke twice says that Mary kept things and pondered them in her heart. After the shepherds came to the stable and told what the angels had said, “Mary kept all these things, pondering them in her heart.” After finding the twelve-year-old Jesus in the Temple, and hearing him say that he must be in his Father’s house, “his mother kept all these things in her heart.”
Mary did not always understand. At the Annunciation she asked, “How can this be?” At the Temple, “they did not understand the saying which he spoke to them.” But she did not push the mystery away. She turned it over and held it. Over decades she watched, remembered, and prayed with what she saw. At Cana, she said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.” At the cross she stood. In the upper room she prayed with the apostles.
The Church sees Mary as the first disciple and the model of contemplation. The Rosary invites us to look at Christ with her eyes.
