units.eq: Why does the Church teach what it teaches?

lessons.title: Sinners in the Church: the abuse crisis and reform
lessons.idea: The Church is holy and made of sinners. When leaders harm the vulnerable or hide it, that is a grave sin that must be faced with truth, justice and care for victims.
lessons.question: How can the Church be holy when some leaders did terrible things?
lessons.activity: List what a safe community looks like (rules, reporting, accountability, care for victims).
teach: Sensitive topic: follow your school’s safe-environment policy and let students step out. Never ask anyone to share personal experiences.

Jesus said it would be better for someone to have a millstone hung around their neck than to cause a little one to stumble (Luke 17:2; Matthew 18:6). Abuse of a minor is a grave sin and a crime. Hiding it makes it worse.

The Church is holy through Christ, but its members, including clergy, are sinners (CCC 823, 827). In the United States the bishops adopted a Charter for the Protection of Children and Young People in 2002 and require safe-environment training and background checks. Reports and reforms continue.

The right response is truth, justice, reporting to civil authorities, care for survivors, and reform. It is not leaving every vulnerable person without the Church’s care, nor pretending nothing happened.
talk: What makes a community safe for children?
Why does covering up a wrong often hurt people more than the original wrong?
How can people stay close to Christ when they are angry with leaders of the Church?
quiz: What did the U.S. bishops adopt in 2002?|A new liturgy|The Charter for the Protection of Children and Young People|A new Catechism|A ban on all youth programs|1|It requires reporting and safe-environment training.
Jesus’ words about those who cause “little ones” to stumble show that…|Only judges can speak of it|Harming children is gravely wrong|It is minor|It should be kept private|1|Luke 17:2.
The Church is “holy” because…|It has never failed|Every member is perfect|Its leaders are sinless|Christ makes it holy, even with sinful members|3|CCC 823.
lessons.life: Learn who to tell if you or a friend is being hurt, and pray for survivors of abuse.
lessons.saint: Peter Damian: a reformer who told popes the truth about the Church’s sin.
misc: “The Church has never dealt with the problem.”
“A few bad priests means everything the Church teaches is false.”
lessons.mem: “Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me.” (Matthew 18:5)
lessons.hook: Say plainly that this lesson is about real harm and real accountability, and that anyone may step out. Follow your diocese’s safe-environment policy.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list what a safe community requires and where to report concerns.

script.open: Say carefully and seriously, “This lesson is about something painful. We’ll speak honestly, with respect for survivors. If you have been hurt by anyone, you are never alone, and you can talk to a trusted adult at any time.” Pause. “Is it hard for people to believe that someone who is supposed to be good can do evil? Why?”
teach: Say: “The Church is holy because Christ is holy, but her members are sinners, including priests and bishops. Jesus chose Judas, and Judas betrayed him. Throughout history, the Church has had scandals and has needed reform. The sexual abuse of minors by clergy is among the worst. Abuse is a grave sin and a crime. It harms victims profoundly, damaging trust, mental health and faith. It betrays the sacred trust that priests have. And the Church’s response was, in many places, inadequate: bishops sometimes moved abusers from parish to parish, hid the cases, and failed to listen to victims.”

Say: “The scale became public in the United States in 2002, when the Boston Globe reported on cases. The John Jay study (2004), commissioned by the bishops, found that about 4 percent of priests serving between 1950 and 2002 were accused, with over 10,000 victims reported, most in the 1960s-1980s. Similar crises came out in Ireland, Australia, Germany, Chile and elsewhere. A Pennsylvania grand jury report in 2018 documented abuse by over 300 priests. The Church has acknowledged these failures. Pope Benedict XVI met with survivors; Pope Francis called the sin and crime ‘a monstrosity’ and acknowledged cover-ups. Victims deserve justice and healing.”

Say: “What reforms have happened? In 2002, the U.S. bishops adopted the Charter for the Protection of Children and Young People, known as the Dallas Charter: zero tolerance for abusers; every diocese must have a victim assistance coordinator and review board; background checks and safe environment training for all clergy, employees and volunteers who work with children; and reporting abuse allegations to civil authorities. In 2019, Pope Francis issued Vos estis lux mundi, requiring clergy to report abuse and creating procedures to investigate bishops. Many dioceses have compensation and counseling programs. The rate of new abuse has fallen sharply. But the Church must remain vigilant. Reform is continuous. In addition, abuse happens in families, schools and sports too, and is a wider problem. What can we do? Know the safe-environment rules; if anyone, in any setting, makes you uncomfortable, tell a trusted adult. Support survivors and believe them. Report. Pray. And hold the Church accountable.”
ask: Is abuse a sin or a crime? (Both.)
What was the Dallas Charter? (A 2002 set of U.S. bishops’ policies: zero tolerance, review boards, background checks, reporting.)
What should a young person do if made uncomfortable? (Tell a trusted adult.)
practice: Work in small groups to write a list of what a safe parish needs: background checks, two adults present, clear reporting, listening to victims, training, transparency.
Write a contact list of trusted adults you could go to.
Write a prayer for survivors.
Discuss: How can the Church rebuild trust?
script.close: Pray for survivors: “Lord, heal those who have been wounded, and purify your Church.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “If you have a concern, speak to a trusted adult.”

tryit: Read the Church’s steps of reform.
Mark which protect children.
Write what a safe community needs.
lessons.saintStory:
Peter Damian was born in Ravenna, Italy, around 1007, the youngest of a large poor family. His brother, a priest, paid for his schooling. He became a brilliant teacher, then entered a hermitage at Fonte Avellana, where he lived a life of prayer and severe penance. In 1043 he became the prior.
The Church of his day was in need of reform: some bishops bought their positions, some priests were not celibate, and the clergy were poorly trained. Peter wrote letters and treatises demanding reform. In about 1049 he wrote the Book of Gomorrah, addressed to Pope Leo IX, which denounced sexual abuse and immorality among the clergy, including the abuse of those they were supposed to serve. He asked the pope to act. Leo IX received it with some sympathy but did not take all the steps Peter asked.
Peter was made a cardinal in 1057, and served as a legate. He died in 1072. He is a Doctor of the Church. He shows that the Church has always needed reform, and that saints have told the truth about it.

lessons.title: Why can’t women be priests?
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that only baptized men are ordained priests, following Christ’s choice of the Twelve, and that this does not mean women are less valuable. Women have always been central to the Church.
lessons.question: Is this fair?
lessons.activity: List the roles of women in the Church, from Mary to the Doctors of the Church.
teach: The Catechism teaches that “only a baptized man validly receives sacred ordination” (CCC 1577), because Christ chose men as apostles and the Church has no authority to change it (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, St John Paul II, 1994).
The Church does not say women are less than men. Equal in dignity (CCC 2334), the sexes have different callings. Mary, the greatest of all the saints, was not a priest.

Women have led the Church as saints, Doctors of the Church (Catherine of Siena, Teresa of Avila, Thérèse of Lisieux, Hildegard of Bingen), abbesses, theologians, missionaries and heads of hospitals and schools.
Many sincerely disagree. Understand the teaching, then discuss respectfully. Some Christian communities have different practices, but the Catholic and Orthodox Churches do not ordain women priests.
talk: What does it mean that people can be equal in dignity and different in roles?
Which woman in the Church’s history do you admire most, and why?
How should we speak with someone who thinks the teaching is unjust?
quiz: Which document restated that the Church cannot ordain women?|Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (1994)|Humanae Vitae|Lumen Fidei|Rerum Novarum|0|St John Paul II.
Who among these is a woman Doctor of the Church?|Monica|Teresa of Avila|Clare of Assisi|Rita|1|Doctors include Teresa of Avila, Catherine of Siena and Thérèse.
The Catechism says the sexes are…|Equal in dignity and different|Identical in every role|Unequal in dignity|Unrelated|0|CCC 2334.
lessons.life: Learn the story of one woman Doctor of the Church and share it.
lessons.saint: Hildegard of Bingen: an abbess whose counsel was sought by popes and emperors.
misc: “Women have no real role in the Church.”
lessons.mem: “Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord.” (Luke 1:38)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Name women who shaped the Church.” List them before addressing the question of ordination.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Church’s reasons for ordaining only men and name three roles women hold.

script.open: Say, “This is a sensitive question that many people have strong feelings about. We will treat each other with respect.” Then ask students to write one question they have about it on a slip and hand it in. Read a few aloud.
teach: Say: “The Catholic Church teaches that priestly ordination is reserved to men. In 1994, Pope John Paul II wrote in Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, ‘The Church has no authority whatsoever to confer priestly ordination on women and this judgment is to be definitively held by all the Church’s faithful.’ The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith said in 1995 that this teaching belongs to the deposit of faith. The reasons are not that women are less than men; the Church insists on the equal dignity of men and women, both made in God’s image.”

Say: “Reasons given. One: Jesus’ example. He chose twelve men as apostles, though he was countercultural in other ways with women: he taught them, he had women disciples, and women were first at the empty tomb. He could have chosen women, but did not. Two: the apostles’ practice. They chose men as successors, including Matthias, Paul, Timothy and Titus. Three: constant Tradition for 2,000 years, in the East and West. Four: the priest acts in persona Christi capitis, in the person of Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church; the sacramental sign reflects the relationship of Christ and the Church, as bridegroom and bride. Five: the Church sees herself bound by Christ’s choice, as she is with the matter of the Eucharist (bread and wine).”

Say: “Some Catholics and many others disagree, saying that the exclusion is cultural. We should be respectful and understand the reasons. Also, the Church teaches that priesthood is not a matter of status or power but of service. Women in the Church have always had great roles. Mary, the Mother of God, is the highest creature, and she was not a priest. There are women Doctors of the Church (Teresa, Catherine, Thérèse, Hildegard), foundresses of orders, missionaries, theologians, teachers, administrators, chancellors, heads of religious orders and Catholic hospitals. Women make up the majority of lay ministers. Pope Francis has appointed women to senior Vatican positions. Regarding women deacons, the Church has studied the question; in the early Church there were deaconesses, such as Phoebe, but their role is debated, and a commission studied it with no consensus. We pray for the Church to discern the Spirit’s will.”
ask: What did John Paul II teach in Ordinatio Sacerdotalis? (The Church has no authority to ordain women.)
Name two reasons given. (Jesus’ choice of twelve men; constant Tradition; the priest acts in the person of Christ.)
Name some roles of women in the Church. (Doctors, foundresses, theologians, lay ministers, Vatican officials.)
practice: Make two columns: “The Church’s reasons” and “Objections and responses.”
Fill in honestly, using the lesson and Ordinatio Sacerdotalis.
Add a list of women saints and their influence.
Write a paragraph: how would I explain this teaching respectfully to a friend who disagrees?
script.close: Pray: “Lord, help us honor the gifts of every member of your Church.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read about a woman Doctor of the Church.”

tryit: List the Church’s reasons for an all-male priesthood.
List the roles women have had in the Church.
Write your own summary.
lessons.saintStory:
Hildegard was born in 1098 in the Rhineland, the tenth child of a noble family, and was given to the Church as a tithe at about eight. She grew up in the care of an anchoress, Jutta, and became a Benedictine nun. She experienced visions from childhood, but kept them secret until she was in her forties, when she began to write them down in Scivias.
She became abbess, founded her own convent at Rupertsberg, and wrote on theology, medicine, natural history, and wrote and composed music for the convent. She corresponded with popes, kings and bishops, including Bernard of Clairvaux, and gave advice (sometimes sharp). She preached in public, which was highly unusual for a woman, traveling on four preaching tours in Germany.
Hildegard died in 1179. In 2012 Pope Benedict XVI named her a Doctor of the Church. She shows that women have held great influence in the Church, although the priesthood is not open to them.

lessons.title: Celibacy: why don’t Catholic priests marry?
lessons.idea: Priestly celibacy is a discipline, not a doctrine, and a gift of undivided love for Christ and the Church. In the Eastern Catholic Churches, married men can be ordained.
lessons.question: Why does the Latin Church ask this of priests?
lessons.activity: Compare the reasons for a celibate priesthood with the reasons for a married one.
teach: Celibacy is a discipline of the Latin Church, not a dogma (CCC 1579–1580). Eastern Catholic priests may be married, though bishops are celibate, and some married former Anglican or Episcopal clergy have been ordained Catholic priests.
Jesus and St Paul both lived and praised chosen celibacy for the Kingdom (Matthew 19:12; 1 Corinthians 7). The Church sees it as total, undivided giving (CCC 1579).

It has costs: loneliness, struggles and failures. The Church asks that men be well formed and supported. The question of whether the discipline should change is a legitimate one, but only the pope and the Church can change it.
Don’t confuse celibacy with the abuse crisis. Most abuse happens in families and many institutions; the answer is accountability and formation.
talk: What might someone gain and lose in giving up marriage for a mission?
Why would the Church treat this as a discipline rather than a doctrine?
How can we support the priests we know?
quiz: Is priestly celibacy a dogma?|It is a law of the Gospels|No, it is a discipline|Yes, an infallible doctrine|It is a sacrament|1|CCC 1579.
Which Catholics may ordain married men as priests?|Only monks|None|Eastern Catholic Churches|Only the Latin Church|2|Eastern practice.
Jesus spoke of those who “make themselves eunuchs” in…|Matthew 19:12|Acts 2:38|Luke 1:28|John 3:16|0|Chosen celibacy for the Kingdom.
lessons.life: Write a thank-you note to a priest or religious who has helped you.
lessons.saint: Solanus Casey: a Capuchin porter whose simple welcome comforted thousands.
misc: “Celibacy is a Church dogma that can never change.”
lessons.mem: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this receive it.” (Matthew 19:12)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you give up for something you loved completely?” Introduce celibacy as a gift with a purpose.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why celibacy is a discipline and where Eastern Catholic priests differ.

script.open: Ask, “Why do you think some people choose not to marry? What might they gain? What might they give up?” Take answers carefully and respectfully.
teach: Say: “In the Latin (Roman) Catholic Church, priests promise celibacy: they don’t marry. In Eastern Catholic Churches, married men may be ordained priests, but they cannot marry after ordination; bishops are chosen from the unmarried. In the Latin Church, married men may become permanent deacons. In some special cases, former Anglican or Lutheran ministers who are married and become Catholic can be ordained priests. So celibacy is a discipline, not a doctrine; the Church could change it, though she has not.”

Say: “The reasons come from Scripture and tradition. Jesus was celibate, and he said, ‘There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He who is able to receive this, let him receive it.’ (Matthew 19:12) Paul, also celibate, wrote that the unmarried man is anxious about the affairs of the Lord, how to please the Lord, whereas the married man is anxious about worldly affairs, how to please his wife (1 Corinthians 7:32-34). Celibacy is a sign of the Kingdom, where ‘they neither marry nor are given in marriage.’ (Matthew 22:30) It lets the priest give his whole heart to God and his people, to be a spiritual father to many. It images Christ, who was celibate and wholly given to the Church.”

Say: “Historically, many early priests were married, but from early centuries the Church encouraged or required continence. The First Lateran Council in 1123 and the Second in 1139 made marriage invalid for priests in the West. The discipline was strengthened at Trent. Critics argue that celibacy discourages vocations and contributes to scandals; the Church answers that celibacy is not the cause of abuse (most abusers in society are not celibate), and the shortage in vocations is also a matter of faith. Celibacy is a gift that must be freely embraced, with grace, prayer, friendships and community. Many priests live it joyfully. It does not mean a priest is not loving. Some priests find it hard, and we should pray for them. The Church also honors married love as holy: marriage is a sacrament.”
ask: Is celibacy a doctrine? (No; it’s a discipline that could change.)
Can married men be priests? (In Eastern Churches, yes; in the Latin Church, only in special cases like former Anglican ministers; permanent deacons can be married.)
What are the reasons for celibacy? (Imitating Christ, undivided service, sign of the Kingdom.)
practice: Make a chart: Reasons for celibacy / Questions and objections / Responses.
Fill in honestly.
Add a row: how the Church honors both marriage and celibacy.
Write a prayer for your parish priest.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, bless our priests and give them joy.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank a priest, and ask him what he loves about his vocation.”

tryit: Read Matthew 19:12 and 1 Corinthians 7:32-35.
Write the reasons for celibacy.
Write the objections and replies.
lessons.saintStory:
Bernard Casey was born in 1870 in Wisconsin, one of sixteen children of Irish immigrants. He worked as a lumberjack, hospital orderly and trolley car operator. After witnessing a violent incident, he felt the call to be a priest. He joined the Capuchin Franciscans, taking the name Solanus.
His seminary studies were hard. He struggled in classes taught in German and Latin, and when he was ordained in 1904, he was allowed to be a “simplex priest,” which meant he could celebrate Mass but not preach doctrinal homilies or hear confessions. He was assigned as a porter, the monastery doorkeeper, in New York, and then in Detroit. For decades he greeted visitors, listened to people with problems, and prayed with them. Many reported healings and graces. During the Depression, he helped start a soup kitchen that fed thousands daily; it is still running.
He died in 1957. He was beatified in 2017. A priest who never preached a sermon became known for the consolation he gave.

units.title: How the faith grows and is handed on
units.eq: How does the Church hand on the faith faithfully?

lessons.title: Development of doctrine
lessons.idea: The Church understands the faith more deeply over time while teaching the same truth. Doctrine develops like a seed growing into a tree, never contradicting what came before.
lessons.question: How can teaching grow without changing?
lessons.activity: Trace the development of one doctrine, like the Trinity or Mary as Mother of God, across councils. Make a timeline showing what was clarified.
teach: The deposit of faith was complete with the apostles (CCC 66, 84). Over time the Church understands it more fully with the help of the Spirit (CCC 94; Dei Verbum 8).
Growth comes through contemplation, study, lived experience and the Magisterium (CCC 94). The Council of Nicaea clarified, not invented, belief in Christ’s divinity.
Newman wrote that a true development preserves the same type and principles; a corruption does not (Essay on Development). Use his seven notes as a guide.
Distinguish doctrine (which develops) from discipline (which can change). Examples: fasting rules, vernacular Mass.
talk: Can you think of a teaching that was clarified over time?
What is the difference between a development and a change?
Why does the Church need a living teacher?
quiz: A true development of doctrine…|Ignores Scripture|Invents a new revelation|Keeps the same truth and deepens it|Reverses an earlier teaching|2|CCC 94.
Who wrote an influential Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine?|Teresa of Ávila|John Henry Newman|Francis de Sales|Thomas Aquinas|1|Newman, 1845.
Which can change?|The resurrection|The Creed|Dogma of the Trinity|Discipline|3|CCC 83.
lessons.life: Pick a doctrine and read how it was explained in a council or a Father.
lessons.saint: John Henry Newman: an Oxford scholar who studied history and became Catholic.
misc: “The Church changes its teaching whenever it wants.”
“Nothing in the faith has ever been explained more deeply.”
lessons.mem: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” (John 16:13)
lessons.hook: Show a seed and a tree. Ask: “Is the tree something new, or the seed grown up?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain development of doctrine and distinguish it from change.

script.open: Pass around a photograph of an oak tree and an acorn. Ask, “Is the tree the same as the acorn? What is different? What stays the same?” Take answers and write them on the board.
teach: Say: “Critics of the Church say her teaching has changed: ‘The Church today teaches things that weren’t taught in the first centuries.’ The Church answers that revelation was complete with Christ and the apostles, but our understanding of it grows. Vatican II said: ‘There is a growth in the understanding of the realities and the words which have been handed down… through the contemplation and study made by believers… through a penetrating understanding of the spiritual realities which they experience… through the preaching of those who have received the sure gift of truth.’ (DV 8)”

Say: “Vincent of Lérins compared this to a human body: it grows and changes, but remains the same person. ‘The religion of souls should imitate the manner of bodies, which, though in the course of years they develop and disclose their members, yet remain the same.’ Newman gave tests for genuine development as opposed to corruption: preservation of type (it’s the same species), continuity of principles, power of assimilation, logical sequence, anticipation of its future, conservative action upon its past, and chronic vigor. A true development clarifies; a corruption contradicts.”

Say: “Examples of development. The Trinity: the New Testament teaches Father, Son and Spirit; the Church worked out the language of ‘one substance, three Persons’ to defend it. The divinity of Christ: held from the start, defined at Nicaea. The canon of Scripture. The Eucharist: from ‘This is my body’ to ‘transubstantiation.’ The Immaculate Conception and the Assumption: implicit in Mary as ‘full of grace’ and the Fathers; defined in 1854 and 1950. The teaching on slavery: always seen as a sin in principle (Paul’s letter to Philemon), but the Church’s moral witness became clearer over time. Religious freedom: Vatican II explained that coercion in matters of faith is contrary to dignity, drawing out something already in the tradition. The Church’s doctrine does not change in meaning but is understood more deeply. As Newman wrote, ‘In a higher world it is otherwise, but here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often.’”
ask: Does doctrine change? (Its meaning does not change; our understanding grows.)
What is the difference between development and corruption? (A development keeps the same principles and clarifies; a corruption contradicts.)
Give an example of development. (The Trinity, the canon, the Assumption.)
practice: Pick one doctrine (Trinity, Real Presence, Mary’s Assumption, or religious freedom).
Trace it in a timeline: Scripture, early Fathers, councils, modern definitions.
Test it against two of Newman’s notes.
Write a paragraph: “How is this the same faith, grown?”
script.close: Pray Newman’s prayer: “Lead, kindly light.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read ‘Lead, Kindly Light.’”

tryit: Test Newman’s seven notes on a doctrine.
Trace one doctrine through the centuries.
Explain how it grew.
lessons.saintStory:
John Henry Newman was born in London in 1801. He became an Anglican priest and a fellow at Oxford, and a leader of the Oxford Movement, which sought to recover the Church of England’s Catholic heritage. His sermons at St. Mary’s drew crowds of students.
As he studied the early Church to defend the Anglican position, he found that the evidence kept pointing to Rome. He wrote, “To be deep in history is to cease to be Protestant.” He puzzled over how the Church today could be the same as the Church of the apostles when so much seemed different. His answer was An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, which he wrote in 1845 and left unfinished when he was received into the Catholic Church on October 9, 1845. It cost him friends and position.
He became a priest, founded the Oratory in Birmingham, and was made a cardinal in 1879. He died in 1890 and was canonized in 2019. His motto: Cor ad cor loquitur, “Heart speaks to heart.”

lessons.title: Dogma and the hierarchy of truths
lessons.idea: Dogmas are truths the Church teaches as revealed by God. Not all truths are equally central: the heart of the faith is the Trinity, Christ and our salvation. All truths belong together.
lessons.question: What is a dogma and why do we have them?
lessons.activity: Sort statements into dogma, doctrine, discipline and opinion. Draw a pyramid with the center of the faith at the top and ordered truths below it.
teach: A dogma is a truth contained in Revelation that the Church defines (CCC 88–90). Dogmas are like lights on the path: they illuminate and secure the faith (CCC 89).
There is an order, or “hierarchy,” of truths (CCC 90; Unitatis Redintegratio 11). The mystery of the Trinity and Christ stand at the center (CCC 234, 426).
Teachings can be defined (dogma), taught definitively, taught authoritatively, or be pastoral guidance. Respond with the appropriate assent (CCC 891–892).
Heresy is the obstinate denial of a revealed truth; it harms unity and faith (CCC 2089).
talk: Why might a Church define a dogma?
What is at the center of our faith?
How can a hierarchy of truths help us in dialogue?
quiz: A dogma is…|A truth the Church defines as revealed|A rule of dress|A song|A feast|0|CCC 88.
At the center of the hierarchy of truths is…|A custom|A building|A holiday|The Trinity and Christ|3|CCC 234.
Heresy is…|A question|Obstinate denial of a revealed truth|A prayer|A doubt|1|CCC 2089.
lessons.life: Choose one dogma and write why it matters for your life.
lessons.saint: Maximus the Confessor: a monk who held to Christ’s two wills though they cut out his tongue.
lessons.mem: “You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” (John 8:32)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What are the rules that cannot change in a game, and which can?” Link to dogma and discipline.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain dogma, hierarchy of truths and heresy.

script.open: Draw a ladder on the board with steps labeled from top to bottom. Say, “Some truths are foundations; others are details. Where would you put the Trinity? The Rosary? Friday abstinence?” Let students place the items.
teach: Say: “A dogma is a truth contained in divine revelation that the Church has defined and proposed as necessary to believe. Dogmas must be believed by all with divine and Catholic faith. They’re not arbitrary rules but signposts that light up and protect the way. The Creed is a summary of dogmas. Dogmas include the Trinity, the Incarnation, the Resurrection, the Real Presence, and the Marian dogmas. Rejecting a dogma knowingly is heresy; the sin of leaving the faith entirely is apostasy; of leaving the Church’s unity is schism. These involve a serious break.”

Say: “Vatican II taught that there is a ‘hierarchy’ of truths, because their connection with the foundation of the Christian faith is different. (Unitatis Redintegratio 11) It does not mean some truths can be ignored. All truths revealed by God must be believed. But some are more central. At the top: the Trinity, the Incarnation and Redemption in Christ, the Paschal Mystery. Closer to the foundation than a particular devotion or discipline. Pope Francis in 2013: ‘The Church’s ministers must be merciful… the proclamation of the saving love of God comes before moral and religious imperatives.’ A good teacher presents the core first.”

Say: “The Church’s teaching has levels. Dogmas of faith (divinely revealed and defined). Definitive doctrines (necessarily connected with revelation, such as the exclusion of women from priesthood or the invalidity of Anglican orders). Authoritative teaching that requires religious assent. Prudential judgments and disciplines (fasting rules, the language of the liturgy, celibacy for the clergy). Customs and devotions (processions, particular prayers). Disciplines can change; dogma cannot. Knowing the difference helps avoid two errors: treating all rules as equally absolute, or treating everything as negotiable. The Creed is central: ‘In essentials, unity; in doubtful matters, liberty; in all things, charity.’”
ask: What is a dogma? (A truth in revelation defined by the Church as necessary to believe.)
What does the hierarchy of truths mean? (Some truths are more central than others, though all must be believed.)
Can disciplines change? (Yes; dogma cannot.)
practice: Prepare a list: the Trinity, meatless Fridays, the Real Presence, Latin Mass, the Assumption, celibacy for priests, the Creed, Marian devotion, the Rosary.
Sort into five levels.
Mark the three most central.
Write why the order matters for explaining the faith.
script.close: Pray the Apostles’ Creed. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pick one line from the Creed and learn its meaning.”

tryit: Sort teachings by level on the hierarchy.
Say which are central.
Explain why order matters.
lessons.saintStory:
Maximus was born around 580 in Constantinople, and served at the imperial court before becoming a monk. He became a great theologian. In the seventh century, a controversy broke out: Monothelitism taught that Christ had only one will, a divine will. The emperor and the patriarch of Constantinople supported it as a compromise to unite the Church. Maximus argued that if Christ lacked a human will, then he had not fully taken on human nature, and our salvation would be incomplete: Christ freely chose to obey the Father, in Gethsemane: “Not my will, but yours.”
Maximus was arrested in 653 and taken to Constantinople. He refused to compromise. In 662, after a trial, his tongue and right hand were cut off, so that he could neither speak nor write against the imperial position. He was exiled to the Caucasus, where he died on August 13, 662. In 681, the Third Council of Constantinople vindicated his teaching: Christ has two wills.
He is called the Confessor, one who suffers for the faith without dying.

lessons.title: The sense of the faithful and the work of the laity in handing on the faith
lessons.idea: All the baptized receive the Spirit and share in handing on the faith. The sense of the faithful, parents, teachers and catechists, and the witness of ordinary people help keep the faith alive.
lessons.question: How do ordinary Catholics hand on the faith?
lessons.activity: Interview a grandparent, catechist or parent about who passed on the faith to them. Write a short thank-you and a plan for passing it on.
teach: The whole body of the faithful, who have an anointing from the Holy One, cannot err in believing (CCC 91–93; 1 John 2:20). This “sense of the faith” works under the guidance of the Magisterium.
The laity share in Christ’s prophetic office by witness and teaching (CCC 904–907). Parents are the first teachers (CCC 2221–2226).
Catechists, teachers, godparents and friends hand on the faith. Women and men have done this since the first generations.
It is not majority opinion. The sense of the faith is discerned by the Church and is linked to Tradition and Scripture.
talk: Who handed the faith to you?
How can you hand on your faith to someone younger?
Why is the sense of the faith not the same as a poll?
quiz: Parents are…|The first teachers of the faith|Only helpers|Replaced by the school|Not involved|0|CCC 2223.
The sense of the faith means…|A vote|The body of the faithful believes the truth under the Spirit|A poll|A feeling|1|CCC 92.
Which is a way to hand on the faith?|Hiding|Silence only|Money|Witness and teaching|3|CCC 905.
lessons.life: Write a note of thanks to someone who passed the faith on to you, and share a prayer with someone younger.
lessons.saint: Juan Diego: a layman who carried the Gospel in his cloak.
lessons.mem: “But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.” (1 John 2:20)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who taught you to pray?” Collect names and notice how many are ordinary people.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the sense of the faith and how they will pass on the faith.

script.open: Ask, “Who passed on your faith to you? Think of one person. Were they a priest?” Take answers. “Most of us learned from a parent, grandparent or teacher.”
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that the faith is handed on in many ways. The Magisterium teaches authoritatively, but the whole Church is involved. Dei Verbum says that Tradition ‘makes progress in the Church… through the contemplation and study made by believers, who treasure these things in their hearts; it comes from the intimate understanding of spiritual things they experience; and it comes from the preaching of those who have received the sure gift of truth.’ The faithful, the laity, have a role. Parents are the first teachers of their children’s faith.”

Say: “The sensus fidei, the sense of the faith, is the supernatural instinct of the whole people of God. Lumen Gentium 12 says: ‘The whole body of the faithful who have an anointing that comes from the holy one cannot err in matters of belief. This characteristic is shown in the supernatural appreciation of the faith (sensus fidei) on the part of the whole people, when, ‘from the bishops down to the last of the lay faithful,’ they manifest a universal consent in matters of faith and morals.’ A famous example: in the fourth century, when many bishops favored Arianism, the ordinary faithful held to the Nicene faith. Newman wrote about this. It doesn’t mean that doctrine is decided by a poll. Public opinion is not the same as the sensus fidei. The sensus fidei is guided by the Spirit and the Magisterium.”

Say: “The laity’s work in handing on the faith is great. Parents teach prayer at home. Godparents and sponsors accompany. Catechists, teachers and youth ministers teach. Lay people serve as readers, extraordinary ministers of Holy Communion, in parish councils, as chaplains and at Catholic hospitals. In the world, the laity bring the Gospel to workplaces, politics and culture. Saints such as Thomas More, Frédéric Ozanam, Pier Giorgio Frassati and Gianna Molla were lay people. The Second Vatican Council taught that the laity share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly roles, and are called to holiness. We are not spectators. Each of us is a link in a chain of faith stretching back to the apostles.”
ask: Who are the first teachers of faith? (Parents.)
What is the sensus fidei? (The Spirit-guided instinct for the faith in the whole people of God.)
Is the sensus fidei a poll? (No; it’s guided by the Spirit and the Magisterium.)
practice: Make a list of everyone who handed on the faith to you.
Draw a chain with your name at the end.
Write three ways you are already handing on the faith, and three you could start.
Choose one to do this month.
script.close: Pray: “Our Lady of Guadalupe, pray for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank the person who taught you to pray.”

tryit: List ways the laity hand on the faith.
Mark the ones you can do now.
Write a plan.
lessons.saintStory:
Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin was born in 1474 near Mexico City, an indigenous Aztec. He and his wife were among the first baptized by the Franciscans in about 1524. In December 1531, as he walked to Mass on Tepeyac Hill, he saw a young woman who spoke to him in his own language, Nahuatl. She said she was the Virgin Mary, and asked him to tell the bishop to build a church there.
The bishop, Juan de Zumárraga, did not believe him and asked for a sign. Juan Diego went back, and Mary told him to gather roses blooming out of season on the hill. He carried them in his tilma, a cloak of cactus fiber, to the bishop. When he opened it, the roses fell out, and on the cloth was an image of the Virgin. The tilma is still preserved at the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, and within a few years millions of Mexicans became Catholic.
Juan Diego lived the rest of his life near the chapel. He was canonized in 2002. Though an ordinary layman, he carried the message.
